title: Set phrases
description: Greetings, thanks, polite formulas, shopping and eating out, what staff say to you, and everyday reactions.

conventions.romaji: kotoba's stored spelling: modified Hepburn, lowercase, no macrons, long vowels as spelled (sou, daijoubu, kirei), wa/o/e particles, っ before ch = t (kotchi). Leading hyphen = attaches to a word.
conventions.register: romaji = casual form, learned first; polite = desu/masu counterpart, or null when there is no register difference.
conventions.freqRank: rank in jiten.moe drama frequency list (CC BY-SA 4.0); freqNote explains tokenizer-split forms. null = no usable rank.
conventions.contrastGroup: items sharing a group name are learned side by side; their examples share a base sentence.

blocks.label: Casual goodbyes
blocks.rationale: Lets you say bye to friends, classmates and coworkers.
blocks.interference: Sayounara sounds final; with friends say mata ne or jaa mata.

items.use: The everyday goodbye between friends and family; answer with mata ne or jaa ne.

example.romaji: jaa, mata ne. kaettara renraku suru.
example.ja: じゃあ、またね。帰ったら連絡する。
example.english: Okay, see you. I'll message you when I get home.

items.notes: Jaa ne is just as common. With people you speak desu/masu to, say shitsurei shimasu instead.

items.use: Said when you'll meet again the next day: classmates, coworkers, friends.

example.romaji: ja, mata ashita. chikoku shinaide ne.
example.ja: じゃ、また明日。遅刻しないでね。
example.english: See you tomorrow. Don't be late.

examplePolite.romaji: mata ashita mo yoroshiku onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: また明日もよろしくお願いします。
examplePolite.english: See you tomorrow, and thanks in advance.

items.notes: Swap in other times: mata raishuu (next week), mata ato de (later today).

items.english: see you then; bye for now
items.use: Said as you split up, often right after making plans, to someone you'll see again.

example.romaji: jaa mata, raishuu no kin'youbi ni ne.
example.ja: じゃあまた、来週の金曜日にね。
example.english: See you then, next Friday.

examplePolite.romaji: dewa mata, kin'youbi ni oai shimashou.
examplePolite.ja: ではまた、金曜日にお会いしましょう。
examplePolite.english: Until Friday, then.

items.notes: With a boss or client, shitsurei shimasu is safer than dewa mata.

items.use: Light, cute goodbye among friends and to kids, usually with a wave.

example.romaji: baibai! mata asobou ne.
example.ja: バイバイ！また遊ぼうね。
example.english: Bye! Let's hang out again.

items.notes: Adults say it too, women more than men; never to a boss or customer.

items.use: Sounds final or formal: teachers and pupils at the end of the school day, or a goodbye for a long time.

example.romaji: minna, sayounara! ki o tsukete kaette ne.
example.ja: みんな、さようなら！気をつけて帰ってね。
example.english: Bye, everyone! Get home safe.

items.notes: Friends rarely say it day to day, and between partners it can sound like a breakup. Use mata ne instead.

blocks.label: Leaving and coming home
blocks.rationale: Lets you do the daily door greetings with family or coworkers.
blocks.interference: Each line has a fixed answer: tadaima gets okaeri, ittekimasu gets itterasshai; don't swap speakers.

items.use: Called out as you walk in the door at home; whoever is in answers okaeri.

example.romaji: tadaima! aa, onaka suita.
example.ja: ただいま！あー、お腹すいた。
example.english: I'm home! Man, I'm starving.

examplePolite.romaji: tadaima modorimashita. nanika arimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: ただいま戻りました。何かありましたか？
examplePolite.english: I'm back. Did anything come up?

items.notes: At work, tadaima modorimashita when you return to the office. In announcements tadaima means 'right now'.

items.use: The answer to tadaima, said by whoever is home; also to a friend back from a trip.

example.romaji: okaeri! gohan dekiteru yo.
example.ja: おかえり！ご飯できてるよ。
example.english: Welcome home! Dinner's ready.

items.notes: Okaerinasai is the fuller, softer form.

items.english: I'm off; see you later (when leaving)
items.use: Said by the person leaving home, or the office for a while; the others answer itterasshai.

example.romaji: jaa, ittekimasu! yuugata ni wa kaeru ne.
example.ja: じゃあ、行ってきます！夕方には帰るね。
example.english: Okay, I'm off! I'll be back by evening.

examplePolite.romaji: ginkou ni ittekimasu. sanjuppun de modorimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 銀行に行ってきます。三十分で戻ります。
examplePolite.english: I'm popping out to the bank. Back in thirty minutes.

items.notes: It stays in -masu even with family. Only when you're coming back; it means 'I'll go and come back'.

items.english: see you later; have a good day (to someone leaving)
items.use: The answer to ittekimasu, said by whoever stays behind; hotel staff say the -mase form to guests heading out.
items.politeJa: いってらっしゃいませ

example.romaji: itterasshai! ame furu kara kasa motte itte ne.
example.ja: いってらっしゃい！雨降るから傘持っていってね。
example.english: See you! It's going to rain, so take an umbrella.

examplePolite.romaji: itterasshaimase. oki o tsukete.
examplePolite.ja: いってらっしゃいませ。お気をつけて。
examplePolite.english: Have a good day. Take care.

items.notes: Not a general goodbye: only to someone who will come back.

items.use: Fuller, warmer form of okaeri; parents, partners, inn staff and coworkers say it to someone returning.

example.romaji: okaerinasai. tsukareta deshou, ofuro waiteru yo.
example.ja: おかえりなさい。疲れたでしょう、お風呂沸いてるよ。
example.english: Welcome home. You must be tired; the bath's ready.

examplePolite.romaji: okaerinasai. shutchou wa ikaga deshita ka?
examplePolite.ja: おかえりなさい。出張はいかがでしたか？
examplePolite.english: Welcome back. How was the business trip?

blocks.label: Greeting and meeting people
blocks.rationale: Lets you say good evening and handle the first questions with someone new.
blocks.interference: Youkoso welcomes you to a place, not into a shop (irasshaimase) or home (okaeri).

items.use: Hello from about sunset on, to neighbours, shop staff or people you don't know well.

example.romaji: konbanwa! mada mise aiteru?
example.ja: こんばんは！まだ店開いてる？
example.english: Evening! Is the shop still open?

examplePolite.romaji: konbanwa. mada aite imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: こんばんは。まだ開いていますか？
examplePolite.english: Good evening. Are you still open?

items.notes: Close friends and family don't say it to each other.

items.use: Short way to ask a name, e.g. at a reception or to a child; answer with your name plus desu.

example.romaji: kawaii ne. onamae wa?
example.ja: かわいいね。お名前は？
example.english: So cute. What's your name?

examplePolite.romaji: shitsurei desu ga, onamae wa nan desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 失礼ですが、お名前は何ですか？
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, but may I ask your name?

items.notes: The o- is only for other people's names; your own is just namae.

items.use: Polite question to someone new about their country or town; answer with the place plus kara desu.

example.romaji: nihongo ojouzu desu ne. dochira kara desu ka?
example.ja: 日本語お上手ですね。どちらからですか？
example.english: Your Japanese is great. Where are you from?

items.notes: Casually: doko kara kita no? It can also mean where have you come from today.

items.use: Welcoming someone to a place, event or group, as in youkoso nihon e; you answer with arigatou or a bow.
items.politeJa: ようこそいらっしゃいました

example.romaji: youkoso, uchi no saakuru e!
example.ja: ようこそ、うちのサークルへ！
example.english: Welcome to our club!

examplePolite.romaji: youkoso irasshaimashita. douzo kochira e.
examplePolite.ja: ようこそいらっしゃいました。どうぞこちらへ。
examplePolite.english: Welcome. This way, please.

items.notes: Not for someone coming home (okaeri) or into a shop (irasshaimase).

blocks.label: Saying thank you
blocks.rationale: Lets you thank staff, friends and anyone who helped.
blocks.interference: Gozaimashita is for help already given; doumo alone can sound curt.

items.use: A quick thanks to staff or someone holding a door; also a nod-like hi to someone you half know.

example.romaji: doumo, hontou ni tasukatta yo.
example.ja: どうも、本当に助かったよ。
example.english: Thanks, that really helped.

examplePolite.romaji: doumo, hontou ni tasukarimashita.
examplePolite.ja: どうも、本当に助かりました。
examplePolite.english: Thank you, that really helped.

items.notes: Alone it can sound curt; doumo arigatou or doumo sumimasen is fuller.

items.use: Thanks for something now finished, like a meal, a lesson or a favour; shop staff say it as you leave.
items.ja: ありがとうございました
items.kana: ありがとうございました

example.romaji: kyou wa hontou ni arigatou gozaimashita.
example.ja: 今日は本当にありがとうございました。
example.english: Thank you so much for today.

items.notes: Arigatou gozaimasu is for help now or still going on; with friends, just arigatou.

items.english: thanks a lot; thank you very much
items.use: Warmer than plain arigatou, to friends, family or someone younger.
items.politeJa: どうもありがとうございます

example.romaji: purezento, doumo arigatou. sugoku ureshii.
example.ja: プレゼント、どうもありがとう。すごく嬉しい。
example.english: Thanks so much for the present. I love it.

examplePolite.romaji: purezento, doumo arigatou gozaimasu. taisetsu ni shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: プレゼント、どうもありがとうございます。大切にします。
examplePolite.english: Thank you so much for the present. I'll treasure it.

items.use: Jokey, light thanks among friends, from the English.

example.romaji: sankyuu! ato de okane kaesu ne.
example.ja: サンキュー！後でお金返すね。
example.english: Thanks! I'll pay you back later.

items.notes: Never to superiors or strangers.

blocks.label: Replying to thanks
blocks.rationale: Lets you answer thanks, apologies or praise.
blocks.interference: Douitashimashite is textbook-stiff; most people say ie ie.

items.use: The everyday reply to thanks, an apology or praise; friendly and fits almost anyone.

example.romaji: ie ie, ki ni shinaide.
example.ja: いえいえ、気にしないで。
example.english: No, no, don't worry about it.

examplePolite.romaji: ie ie, ki ni shinaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: いえいえ、気にしないでください。
examplePolite.english: Not at all, please don't worry about it.

items.notes: Far more common in real life than douitashimashite.

items.use: The textbook reply to thanks; real speakers often prefer ie ie, which sounds less stiff.

example.romaji: douitashimashite. mata nanka attara itte ne.
example.ja: どういたしまして。またなんかあったら言ってね。
example.english: You're welcome. Let me know if you need anything else.

examplePolite.romaji: douitashimashite. mata nanika attara itsu demo itte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: どういたしまして。また何かあったらいつでも言ってください。
examplePolite.english: You're welcome. Just ask anytime you need something.

items.notes: Can sound as if you agree you did a big favour.

items.english: not at all (reply to thanks or praise); outrageous
items.use: A humble brush-off of thanks or praise, stronger than ie ie.

example.romaji: tondemonai, tasukerareta no wa kotchi da yo.
example.ja: とんでもない、助けられたのはこっちだよ。
example.english: Not at all, you're the one who helped me.

examplePolite.romaji: tondemonai desu. kochira koso tasukarimashita.
examplePolite.ja: とんでもないです。こちらこそ助かりました。
examplePolite.english: Not at all. You helped me more.

items.notes: Before a noun it means outrageous or terrible: tondemonai koto ni natta (things got crazy).

blocks.label: Saying sorry
blocks.rationale: Lets you apologize for being late, a slip or a mistake.
blocks.interference: Doumo sumimasen can be thanks as well as sorry; gomen gomen is too light for anything serious.

items.use: A sincere personal apology to family, friends or a partner; children use it with anyone.

example.romaji: gomen nasai, kinou no yakusoku wasureteta.
example.ja: ごめんなさい、昨日の約束忘れてた。
example.english: I'm sorry, I forgot our plans yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: gomen nasai, kinou no yakusoku o wasurete imashita.
examplePolite.ja: ごめんなさい、昨日の約束を忘れていました。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry, I forgot about yesterday's appointment.

items.notes: Gomen alone is the casual short form. At work or with strangers, sumimasen fits better.

items.use: Apologizing for something already done, like a mistake at work or being rude.

example.romaji: kinou wa sumimasen deshita. chotto iisugimashita.
example.ja: 昨日はすみませんでした。ちょっと言いすぎました。
example.english: Sorry about yesterday. I said too much.

items.notes: Plain sumimasen also means excuse me and thanks; the -deshita form is only an apology.

items.use: Quick, breezy apology to a friend for something small, like being a bit late.

example.romaji: gomen gomen, densha okureta.
example.ja: ごめんごめん、電車遅れた。
example.english: Sorry, sorry, my train was late.

items.notes: Too light for anything serious; it can sound like you don't care.

items.english: I'm so sorry; thank you so much
items.use: A stronger sumimasen to staff, strangers or anyone you've put out: a real apology, or thanks that admits you caused trouble.

example.romaji: wazawaza todokete kudasatte, doumo sumimasen.
example.ja: わざわざ届けてくださって、どうもすみません。
example.english: Thank you so much for bringing it all this way.

items.notes: The situation tells you whether it's thanks or sorry; often it's both.

items.english: sorry I'm late; sorry for the slow reply
items.use: Said on arriving late, or at the start of a late reply to a message or email.
items.ja: 遅くなってすみません
items.kana: おそくなってすみません

example.romaji: osoku natte sumimasen, michi ga konde imashita.
example.ja: 遅くなってすみません、道が混んでいました。
example.english: Sorry I'm late, the roads were busy.

items.notes: With friends: osoku natte gomen. For a message: henji ga osoku natte sumimasen.

blocks.label: Asking if it's okay
blocks.rationale: Lets you ask permission, from casual to very polite.
blocks.interference: Ii desu ka asks permission; ii no? checks someone means their offer.

items.use: Asks permission or checks something is fine; put the thing first (koko, ii desu ka?) or a -te mo verb (suwatte mo ii desu ka?).

example.romaji: sumimasen, koko suwatte mo ii desu ka?
example.ja: すみません、ここ座ってもいいですか？
example.english: Excuse me, is it okay if I sit here?

items.notes: Casual is just ii? with a rising tone. Yes is hai, douzo; a no usually starts with chotto...

items.english: would that be all right?; may I?
items.use: Very polite ii desu ka; you hear it from staff checking an order, and can use it with bosses and strangers.

example.romaji: kochira de yoroshii desu ka?
example.ja: こちらでよろしいですか？
example.english: Will this one be all right?

items.notes: Staff also say yoroshii deshou ka, softer still.

items.use: Lead-in before a personal or awkward question.

example.romaji: chotto kiite mo ii? kanojo iru?
example.ja: ちょっと聞いてもいい？彼女いる？
example.english: Can I ask you something? Do you have a girlfriend?

examplePolite.romaji: hitotsu kiite mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 一つ聞いてもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: Can I ask you one thing?

items.notes: Very polite version: ukagatte mo yoroshii desu ka.

blocks.label: Deciding what to do
blocks.rationale: Lets you ask what to do, agree on a plan and say you don't mind.
blocks.interference: Dou suru? asks what we'll do; dou shitara ii? asks for advice when stuck.

items.english: what do you want to do?; what shall we do?
items.use: Asks a friend to decide or pick between options; answer with your choice plus ni suru, or dotchi demo ii.

example.romaji: ame da kedo, dou suru? ie de eiga miru?
example.ja: 雨だけど、どうする？家で映画見る？
example.english: It's raining. What do you want to do? Watch a movie at home?

examplePolite.romaji: ame desu ne. dou shimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 雨ですね。どうしますか？
examplePolite.english: It's raining. What shall we do?

items.notes: Dou shiyou (what do I do?) is the worried version you say to yourself.

items.use: Asks someone for advice when you're stuck or don't know the next step.
items.politeJa: どうしたらいいですか

example.romaji: kagi nakushichatta. dou shitara ii?
example.ja: 鍵なくしちゃった。どうしたらいい？
example.english: I lost my keys. What should I do?

examplePolite.romaji: kagi o nakushite shimatta n desu ga, dou shitara ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 鍵をなくしてしまったんですが、どうしたらいいですか？
examplePolite.english: I've lost my key. What should I do?

items.notes: Dou sureba ii? means the same.

items.use: Agrees to a plan someone just suggested.

example.romaji: ii ne, sou shiyou!
example.ja: いいね、そうしよう！
example.english: Good idea, let's do that!

examplePolite.romaji: ii desu ne. sou shimashou.
examplePolite.ja: いいですね。そうしましょう。
examplePolite.english: Sounds good. Let's do that.

items.notes: Sou suru (I'll do that) is about your own action only, e.g. when you take someone's advice.

items.use: Tells someone you don't mind which; add yo to sound easygoing rather than bored.

example.romaji: ramen demo sushi demo, dotchi demo ii yo.
example.ja: ラーメンでも寿司でも、どっちでもいいよ。
example.english: Ramen or sushi, either's fine with me.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi wa dochira demo ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 私はどちらでもいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Either is fine with me.

items.notes: Said flatly it can sound like you don't care. Nan demo ii means anything is fine.

items.use: Settles a plan or choice someone just suggested; to staff add onegai shimasu.
items.politeJa: じゃあそれでお願いします

example.romaji: rokuji ni eki? un, jaa sore de.
example.ja: 6時に駅？うん、じゃあそれで。
example.english: Six at the station? Okay, let's go with that.

examplePolite.romaji: jaa, sore de onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: じゃあ、それでお願いします。
examplePolite.english: Okay, I'll go with that, please.

blocks.label: Choosing what to buy
blocks.rationale: Lets you pick an item, ask for advice and try clothes on.
blocks.interference: Kore kudasai points at a thing; kore ni shimasu announces a decision after comparing.

items.english: I'll take this one; I'll have this
items.use: Tells staff your choice after looking or comparing; works for food orders too.

example.romaji: jaa, kore ni shimasu.
example.ja: じゃあ、これにします。
example.english: Okay, I'll go with this one.

items.notes: X ni suru means decide on X. Casual version: kore ni suru.

items.use: The simplest way to buy or order: point at the thing at a counter, stall or menu.

example.romaji: kore to kore, kudasai.
example.ja: これとこれ、ください。
example.english: This and this, please.

items.notes: Add a count: kore futatsu kudasai (two of these).

items.use: Ask staff at a restaurant or shop; casual version is osusume wa?
items.kana: おすすめはなんですか

example.romaji: sumimasen, osusume wa nan desu ka?
example.ja: すみません、おすすめは何ですか？
example.english: Excuse me, what do you recommend?

items.notes: Menus mark recommended dishes as osusume.

items.romaji: shichaku shite mo ii desu ka
items.use: Ask a clothes-shop assistant before taking things to the fitting room (shichakushitsu).
items.ja: 試着してもいいですか
items.kana: しちゃくしてもいいですか

example.romaji: sumimasen, kore shichaku shite mo ii desu ka?
example.ja: すみません、これ試着してもいいですか？
example.english: Excuse me, can I try this on?

items.notes: Staff usually answer douzo, kochira e (sure, this way).

blocks.label: Price and paying
blocks.rationale: Lets you ask the price, check the tax and pay by card.
blocks.interference: Kaado tsukaemasu ka asks if cards work; kaado de onegai shimasu chooses card.

items.use: Point at or name the item first: kore, ikura desu ka?

example.romaji: sumimasen, kore ikura desu ka?
example.ja: すみません、これいくらですか？
example.english: Excuse me, how much is this?

items.notes: Casual version: ikura? Prices come back as numbers plus en: sen en is 1,000 yen.

items.use: Answer at the till when staff ask how you'll pay (oshiharai wa?).
items.ja: カードでお願いします
items.kana: カードでおねがいします

example.romaji: a, kaado de onegai shimasu.
example.ja: あ、カードでお願いします。
example.english: Oh, by card, please.

items.notes: Cash is genkin de. If staff ask ikkai barai de yoroshii desu ka (one payment?), just say hai.

items.use: Ask before ordering or at the till; small places may be cash only.

example.romaji: sumimasen, kaado tsukaemasu ka?
example.ja: すみません、カード使えますか？
example.english: Excuse me, do you take cards?

items.notes: Genkin dake desu means cash only.

items.use: Checks a price tag or quote; prices are shown either with tax (zeikomi) or without (zeinuki).

example.romaji: kono nedan, zeikomi desu ka?
example.ja: この値段、税込みですか？
example.english: Does this price include tax?

items.use: Said when the cashier hands over or offers the receipt.
items.ja: レシートは大丈夫です
items.kana: レシートはだいじょうぶです

example.romaji: reshiito wa daijoubu desu. arigatou gozaimasu.
example.ja: レシートは大丈夫です。ありがとうございます。
example.english: I don't need the receipt. Thank you.

items.notes: A formal receipt for expenses is a ryoushuusho.

blocks.label: Bags and wrapping
blocks.rationale: Lets you answer the bag and wrapping questions at every till.
blocks.interference: Daijoubu desu here means no thanks, not yes.

items.use: Answer when the cashier asks if you want a bag; daijoubu here means no thanks.
items.kana: ふくろはだいじょうぶです

example.romaji: a, fukuro wa daijoubu desu.
example.ja: あ、袋は大丈夫です。
example.english: Oh, I don't need a bag.

items.notes: Bags cost a few yen, so you'll be asked at most tills.

items.use: Asks for a bag at the till; it usually costs a few yen.
items.kana: ふくろおねがいします

example.romaji: fukuro onegai shimasu. hitotsu de ii desu.
example.ja: 袋お願いします。一つでいいです。
example.english: A bag, please. Just one is fine.

items.use: Tells staff you don't need a bag, wrapping or a box; also works for anything you'd leave unchanged.

example.romaji: sugu tsukau node, kono mama de ii desu.
example.ja: すぐ使うので、このままでいいです。
example.english: I'll use it right away, so it's fine as it is.

items.notes: Kono mama means like this, unchanged.

items.use: Tells staff the item is a present so they wrap it; they often ask gojitaku you desu ka? (is it for yourself?) first.

example.romaji: purezento you desu. tsutsunde moraemasu ka?
example.ja: プレゼント用です。包んでもらえますか？
example.english: It's a present. Could you wrap it?

items.notes: Here -you means for, not seems.

blocks.label: Hungry tasty and full
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about hunger and food before, during and after a meal.
blocks.interference: Oishisou is before eating, oishikatta after; tabesugita and mou taberarenai both mean you're full but only the second refuses more.

items.use: Everyday way to say you're hungry; Japanese says it in the past form.

example.romaji: aa, onaka suita. nanika tabeyou.
example.ja: あー、お腹すいた。何か食べよう。
example.english: Ugh, I'm hungry. Let's eat something.

examplePolite.romaji: onaka sukimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: お腹すきましたね。
examplePolite.english: I'm getting hungry, aren't you?

items.notes: Ask others with onaka suiteru? (are you hungry?). Men may say hara hetta.

items.use: Said when food arrives or you see it, before eating; after eating say oishii or oishikatta.

example.romaji: uwa, oishisou! itadakimasu.
example.ja: うわ、おいしそう！いただきます。
example.english: Wow, that looks so good! Let's eat.

examplePolite.romaji: oishisou desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: おいしそうですね。
examplePolite.english: That looks delicious.

items.notes: -sou on an adjective means looks: takasou (looks expensive). Ii becomes yosasou (looks good).

items.use: Said after finishing a meal; to a host or staff, follow with gochisousama deshita.

example.romaji: aa, oishikatta. gochisousama!
example.ja: あー、おいしかった。ごちそうさま！
example.english: Mm, that was delicious. Thanks for the meal!

examplePolite.romaji: totemo oishikatta desu. gochisousama deshita.
examplePolite.ja: とてもおいしかったです。ごちそうさまでした。
examplePolite.english: That was really delicious. Thank you for the meal.

items.use: Groaned after a big meal; half complaint, half compliment to the cook.

example.romaji: aa, tabesugita. onaka ippai.
example.ja: あー、食べ過ぎた。お腹いっぱい。
example.english: Ugh, I ate too much. I'm stuffed.

examplePolite.romaji: oishikute, tabesugimashita.
examplePolite.ja: おいしくて、食べ過ぎました。
examplePolite.english: It was so good I ate too much.

items.notes: Onaka ippai means I'm full.

items.use: Said when you're full and someone offers more.

example.romaji: gomen, mou taberarenai. onaka ippai.
example.ja: ごめん、もう食べられない。お腹いっぱい。
example.english: Sorry, I can't eat any more. I'm stuffed.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, mou taberaremasen.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、もう食べられません。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I couldn't eat another thing.

items.notes: Many speakers drop the ra: mou taberenai.

blocks.label: Asking restaurant staff
blocks.rationale: Lets you get seated, order, ask for water and the toilet, and finish ordering.
blocks.interference: Ijou desu ends your order; it doesn't ask for the bill.

items.use: Calls staff over when you're ready to order; start with sumimasen!
items.kana: ちゅうもんいいですか

example.romaji: sumimasen, chuumon ii desu ka?
example.ja: すみません、注文いいですか？
example.english: Excuse me, can we order?

items.notes: Many places have a call button on the table instead.

items.use: Ends your order at a restaurant or counter; staff and speakers also use it to end a talk or report.

example.romaji: biiru futatsu to edamame, ijou desu.
example.ja: ビール二つと枝豆、以上です。
example.english: Two beers and edamame. That's all.

items.notes: Staff may check with ijou de yoroshii desu ka? (will that be all?).

items.use: Ask staff in shops, restaurants and stations; casual is toire doko?

example.romaji: sumimasen, toire wa doko desu ka?
example.ja: すみません、トイレはどこですか？
example.english: Excuse me, where's the toilet?

items.notes: Otearai is a politer word for toilet. At someone's home: toire karite mo ii desu ka?

items.english: two people; a table for two
items.use: Answer at the restaurant door when staff ask nanmeisama desu ka? (how many?).

example.romaji: futari desu. kauntaa demo ii desu.
example.ja: 二人です。カウンターでもいいです。
example.english: Two of us. The counter's fine.

items.notes: One is hitori desu, three is sannin desu. Holding up fingers works too.

items.use: Asks staff for water; it's free, and some places have you pour it yourself (serufu saabisu).

example.romaji: sumimasen, omizu futatsu kudasai.
example.ja: すみません、お水二つください。
example.english: Excuse me, two waters, please.

blocks.label: Eat in or take out
blocks.rationale: Lets you answer the counter's eat-in question and size up a bowl.
blocks.interference: Tennai de is eating here, mochikaeri de is taking it away.

items.use: Answer at a cafe or fast-food counter when staff ask if you're eating in (tennai de omeshiagari desu ka?).
items.politeJa: 持ち帰りでお願いします

example.romaji: kore, mochikaeri de.
example.ja: これ、持ち帰りで。
example.english: This one to go.

examplePolite.romaji: mochikaeri de onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 持ち帰りでお願いします。
examplePolite.english: To take away, please.

items.notes: Staff say omochikaeri; chains also use teikuauto.

items.english: to eat in, please; for here
items.use: Answer at a cafe or fast-food counter when asked if you're eating here; the opposite is mochikaeri de.

example.romaji: tennai de, aisu koohii hitotsu.
example.ja: 店内で、アイスコーヒー一つ。
example.english: For here, one iced coffee.

examplePolite.romaji: tennai de onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 店内でお願いします。
examplePolite.english: For here, please.

items.use: Asks for an extra-large serving of rice or noodles, often for a small extra charge.
items.politeJa: 大盛りでお願いします

example.romaji: gyuudon hitotsu, oomori de.
example.ja: 牛丼一つ、大盛りで。
example.english: One beef bowl, large.

examplePolite.romaji: gohan wa oomori de onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: ご飯は大盛りでお願いします。
examplePolite.english: A large serving of rice, please.

items.notes: Normal size is namimori; a smaller one is sukuname.

blocks.label: What shop staff say
blocks.rationale: Lets you recognise the greetings and replies staff use every time you buy or order.
blocks.interference: Gochuumon and okoshi are staff words; for yourself say chuumon and ukagaimasu.

items.use: Staff's reply when they take your order or request; no answer needed.

example.romaji: kashikomarimashita. shoushou omachi kudasai.
example.ja: かしこまりました。少々お待ちください。
example.english: Certainly. One moment, please.

items.notes: At work you can say it to a boss or client; wakarimashita is the everyday version.

items.use: Called out by staff as you walk into a shop or restaurant; customers don't reply, a nod is enough.

example.romaji: irasshaimase! nanmeisama desu ka?
example.ja: いらっしゃいませ！何名様ですか？
example.english: Welcome! How many in your party?

items.notes: At someone's home you'll hear irasshai (come on in).

items.use: Staff's polite word for your order; for your own order you just say chuumon.

example.romaji: gochuumon wa okimari desu ka?
example.ja: ご注文はお決まりですか？
example.english: Are you ready to order?

items.notes: To ask for more time: mou sukoshi matte kudasai.

items.use: Staff and hosts use it about your coming: yoku okoshi kudasaimashita (thanks for coming), mata no okoshi o omachi shite orimasu (please come again).

example.romaji: mata no okoshi o omachi shite orimasu.
example.ja: またのお越しをお待ちしております。
example.english: We look forward to seeing you again.

items.notes: Never use it about yourself; for your own visit say ukagaimasu.

blocks.label: Waiting your turn
blocks.rationale: Lets you follow staff when you're asked to wait, called forward or served.
blocks.interference: Omatase shimashita (sorry for the wait) and omachi kudasai (please wait) share a verb but come at opposite moments.

items.use: Staff say it before checking something or going to get it; just say hai and wait.
items.kana: しょうしょうおまちください

example.romaji: zaiko o kakunin shimasu node, shoushou omachi kudasai.
example.ja: 在庫を確認しますので、少々お待ちください。
example.english: I'll check our stock, so one moment, please.

items.notes: The casual version is chotto matte. On the phone it means you're being put on hold.

items.english: sorry to keep you waiting; here you are
items.use: Staff say it when they bring your order or come back to you, even after a short wait.

example.romaji: omatase shimashita. raamen to gyouza desu.
example.ja: お待たせしました。ラーメンと餃子です。
example.english: Here you are. Ramen and gyoza.

items.notes: Say it yourself when you join someone who has been waiting; with friends just omatase.

items.use: Called out at a counter, register or clinic when it's your turn; step forward.

example.romaji: omatase shimashita. tsugi no kata douzo.
example.ja: お待たせしました。次の方どうぞ。
example.english: Thanks for waiting. Next, please.

items.notes: Kata is the polite word for person, as in ano kata (that person).

items.english: this register, please; I can help you over here
items.use: A cashier opening another till calls the next customer over; go to that register.
items.ja: こちらのレジへどうぞ
items.kana: こちらのレジへどうぞ

example.romaji: otsugi no okyakusama, kochira no reji e douzo.
example.ja: お次のお客様、こちらのレジへどうぞ。
example.english: Next customer, over at this register, please.

items.notes: Reji means the cash register or checkout.

items.english: I'll be right with you; coming right away
items.use: Staff call it back when you say sumimasen! and they're busy; just wait a moment.
items.kana: ただいまうかがいます

example.romaji: hai, tadaima ukagaimasu. shoushou omachi kudasai!
example.ja: はい、ただいま伺います。少々お待ちください！
example.english: Yes, I'll be right with you. One moment, please!

items.notes: Tadaima here means right now, not the I'm-home greeting. Ukagau is the humble verb for come or visit.

blocks.label: Getting a table
blocks.rationale: Lets you get from the restaurant door to your seat.
blocks.interference: Omachi shite orimashita (we expected you) sounds like omachi kudasai (please wait).

items.english: how many people?; how many in your party?
items.use: The first thing restaurant staff ask; answer with the number, hitori desu or futari desu, and hold up fingers.

example.romaji: irasshaimase. nanmeisama desu ka?
example.ja: いらっしゃいませ。何名様ですか？
example.english: Welcome. How many people?

items.notes: Also heard as nanmeisama deshou ka. Watch the counting: hitori, futari, then sannin, yonin.

items.use: Staff say it while leading you to a seat or room; just follow them.

example.romaji: oseki e goannai shimasu. kochira e douzo.
example.ja: お席へご案内します。こちらへどうぞ。
example.english: I'll show you to your table. This way, please.

items.notes: You can say it too when guiding a guest. Kochira is the polite word for this way (casual kotchi).

items.use: Staff say it when there are free tables; just pick one.
items.kana: おすきなせきへどうぞ

example.romaji: ohitori desu ne. osuki na seki e douzo.
example.ja: お一人ですね。お好きな席へどうぞ。
example.english: Just one? Sit anywhere you like.

items.use: Asked at a restaurant door or hotel desk; answer hai, then your name + desu, or iie.
items.ja: ご予約はされていますか
items.kana: ごよやくはされていますか

example.romaji: irasshaimase. goyoyaku wa sarete imasu ka?
example.ja: いらっしゃいませ。ご予約はされていますか？
example.english: Welcome. Do you have a reservation?

items.notes: Also heard as goyoyaku wa gozaimasu ka?

items.use: Hotel or restaurant staff say it once they confirm your booking; a nod or yoroshiku onegai shimasu is fine.
items.ja: お待ちしておりました
items.kana: おまちしておりました

example.romaji: tanaka-sama desu ne. omachi shite orimashita.
example.ja: 田中様ですね。お待ちしておりました。
example.english: Mr. Tanaka? We've been expecting you.

items.notes: The casual equivalent between friends is matteta yo (I was waiting for you).

blocks.label: Ordering a meal
blocks.rationale: Lets you follow the waiter from ordering to clearing the plates.
blocks.interference: Gochuumon wa okimari (ready to order?) and gochuumon wa ijou (is that all?) start the same way.

items.english: enjoy your meal; enjoy your stay; take your time
items.use: Staff say it after serving food or showing you to a room; no reply needed, a nod or doumo is fine.

example.romaji: kochira koohii desu. goyukkuri douzo.
example.ja: こちらコーヒーです。ごゆっくりどうぞ。
example.english: Here's your coffee. Enjoy.

items.notes: Often shortened to just goyukkuri. A host says it to guests at home too.

items.use: A waiter asks when they come to the table; answer hai, or mou sukoshi (a little more time).
items.ja: ご注文はお決まりですか
items.kana: ごちゅうもんはおきまりですか

example.romaji: shitsurei shimasu. gochuumon wa okimari desu ka?
example.ja: 失礼します。ご注文はお決まりですか？
example.english: Excuse me. Are you ready to order?

items.notes: In many places you call the waiter yourself with sumimasen! or a call button on the table.

items.romaji: gochuumon wa ijou de yoroshii desu ka
items.english: will that be all?; is that everything?
items.use: Staff check after you order; answer hai, or add something.
items.ja: ご注文は以上でよろしいですか
items.kana: ごちゅうもんはいじょうでよろしいですか

example.romaji: kashikomarimashita. gochuumon wa ijou de yoroshii desu ka?
example.ja: かしこまりました。ご注文は以上でよろしいですか？
example.english: Certainly. Will that be all?

items.notes: Often shortened to ijou de yoroshii desu ka? Ijou means that's all.

items.english: what would you like to drink?; would you like a drink?
items.use: A waiter asks after you order food; answer X o onegai shimasu, or kekkou desu (no thanks).
items.ja: お飲み物はいかがなさいますか
items.kana: おのみものはいかがなさいますか

example.romaji: onomimono wa ikaga nasaimasu ka? hotto to aisu ga gozaimasu.
example.ja: お飲み物はいかがなさいますか？ホットとアイスがございます。
example.english: What would you like to drink? We have hot or iced.

items.notes: Ikaga nasaimasu ka (how would you like it?) also comes with other choices, like size or sauce.

items.romaji: osage shite mo yoroshii desu ka
items.english: may I take your plate?; may I clear this?
items.use: A waiter asks before clearing dishes; answer hai, onegai shimasu, or mada desu (not yet).
items.ja: お下げしてもよろしいですか
items.kana: おさげしてもよろしいですか

example.romaji: kochira, osage shite mo yoroshii desu ka?
example.ja: こちら、お下げしてもよろしいですか？
example.english: May I take this away?

items.notes: Sageru here means to clear away.

blocks.label: For here or to go
blocks.rationale: Lets you answer the quick questions at fast-food and convenience-store counters.
blocks.interference: Tennai (eat in) and mochikaeri (take home) both expect a plain hai, so listen for which one was asked.

items.english: for here?; are you eating in?
items.use: Asked at fast-food and café counters; answer hai, or mochikaeri de (to go).
items.ja: 店内でお召し上がりですか
items.kana: てんないでおめしあがりですか

example.romaji: tennai de omeshiagari desu ka, omochikaeri desu ka?
example.ja: 店内でお召し上がりですか、お持ち帰りですか？
example.english: For here or to go?

items.notes: Meshiagaru is the respectful verb for eat and drink.

items.use: Asked at fast-food, café and bento counters; answer hai, or tennai de (for here).

example.romaji: omochikaeri desu ka? fukuro ni oire shimasu ne.
example.ja: お持ち帰りですか？袋にお入れしますね。
example.english: To go? I'll put it in a bag.

items.notes: To ask for it yourself, say mochikaeri de onegai shimasu. Some places say teikuauto.

items.use: Convenience-store staff ask about bento and other food; answer onegai shimasu, or daijoubu desu (no thanks).

example.romaji: kochira no obentou, atatamemasu ka?
example.ja: こちらのお弁当、温めますか？
example.english: Shall I heat up this bento?

items.notes: Also heard as oatatame shimasu ka? Daijoubu desu here means no thanks.

items.use: Asked at convenience stores and takeout counters; answer onegai shimasu, or daijoubu desu (no thanks).
items.ja: お箸はお付けしますか
items.kana: おはしはおつけしますか

example.romaji: obentou futatsu desu ne. ohashi wa otsuke shimasu ka?
example.ja: お弁当二つですね。お箸はお付けしますか？
example.english: Two bentos, right? Do you need chopsticks?

items.notes: The same pattern comes for spoons: supuun wa otsuke shimasu ka?

blocks.label: Checkout questions
blocks.rationale: Lets you get through the questions at almost any shop register.
blocks.interference: Daijoubu desu here means no thanks, not yes.

items.use: Cashiers ask because bags cost a few yen; answer onegai shimasu, or daijoubu desu (no thanks).
items.kana: ふくろはおつけしますか

example.romaji: fukuro wa otsuke shimasu ka? san en ni narimasu.
example.ja: 袋はお付けしますか？3円になります。
example.english: Do you need a bag? It's 3 yen.

items.notes: Also heard as fukuro wa goriyou desu ka? or fukuro irimasu ka?

items.romaji: pointo kaado wa omochi desu ka
items.english: do you have a points card?
items.use: Asked at almost every register; answer nai desu, or hand the card over.
items.ja: ポイントカードはお持ちですか
items.kana: ポイントカードはおもちですか

example.romaji: irasshaimase. pointo kaado wa omochi desu ka?
example.ja: いらっしゃいませ。ポイントカードはお持ちですか？
example.english: Hello. Do you have a points card?

items.notes: Omochi desu ka (do you have?) also comes up for tickets, coupons and receipts.

items.english: how would you like to pay?
items.use: Asked at the register; answer kaado de, genkin de (cash), or an app name + de.
items.ja: お支払いはどうされますか
items.kana: おしはらいはどうされますか

example.romaji: zenbu de sanzen en desu. oshiharai wa dou saremasu ka?
example.ja: 全部で3000円です。お支払いはどうされますか？
example.english: That's 3,000 yen altogether. How would you like to pay?

items.notes: Also heard as oshiharai houhou wa? (payment method?).

items.english: is a sticker okay? (instead of a bag)
items.use: When you buy one small item, the cashier offers to mark it paid with a sticker instead of bagging it; answer hai.

example.romaji: kochira, shiiru de ii desu ka?
example.ja: こちら、シールでいいですか？
example.english: Is a sticker okay for this?

items.notes: Also heard as teepu de yoroshii desu ka? (tape).

blocks.label: On my way
blocks.rationale: Lets you ask where someone is and report your progress when meeting up.
blocks.interference: Tsuita yo (I'm here) and mou sugu tsuku (almost there) differ only in tense.

items.use: The standard text or call when meeting up; answer with a place + da yo, or ima mukatteru.

example.romaji: ima doko? mou eki ni tsuita yo.
example.ja: 今どこ？もう駅に着いたよ。
example.english: Where are you? I'm already at the station.

examplePolite.romaji: ima doko desu ka? kaisatsu no mae ni imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今どこですか？改札の前にいます。
examplePolite.english: Where are you now? I'm in front of the ticket gates.

items.notes: To someone senior, ima dochira desu ka sounds more polite.

items.use: Texted or said when someone asks where you are; add a place + ni to say where you're heading.

example.romaji: ima mukatteru! juppun gurai de tsuku.
example.ja: 今向かってる！10分ぐらいで着く。
example.english: I'm on my way! I'll be there in about ten minutes.

examplePolite.romaji: ima eki ni mukatte imasu. sugu tsukimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今駅に向かっています。すぐ着きます。
examplePolite.english: I'm heading to the station now. I'll be there soon.

items.notes: Mukau means head toward. Ima iku is closer to I'm coming right now.

items.use: Texted or said when you reach the meeting place; add where: eki ni tsuita yo.

example.romaji: tsuita yo. kitaguchi no mae ni iru.
example.ja: 着いたよ。北口の前にいる。
example.english: I'm here. I'm in front of the north exit.

examplePolite.romaji: ima tsukimashita. iriguchi no mae ni imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今着きました。入口の前にいます。
examplePolite.english: I just got here. I'm in front of the entrance.

items.notes: Past tense because you've already arrived. Mou tsuita? means are you there yet?

items.use: Texted or said when you're close; often with yo, or kara to mean so hang on.

example.romaji: mou sugu tsuku yo. ato gofun.
example.ja: もうすぐ着くよ。あと5分。
example.english: I'm almost there. Five more minutes.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, mou sugu tsukimasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、もうすぐ着きます。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I'm almost there.

items.notes: Mou sugu means very soon and works with other verbs: mou sugu owaru (almost done).

blocks.label: Late and waiting
blocks.rationale: Lets you apologize for being late and handle the moment you meet up.
blocks.interference: Okurete gomen (I was late) versus chotto okureru (I will be late).

items.english: sorry to keep you waiting; here I am
items.use: Said when you reach a friend who has been waiting, even a minute; they often answer zenzen (not at all).

example.romaji: gomen, omatase! ikou ka.
example.ja: ごめん、お待たせ！行こうか。
example.english: Sorry to keep you waiting! Shall we go?

examplePolite.romaji: omatase shimashita. sumimasen, densha ga okurete.
examplePolite.ja: お待たせしました。すみません、電車が遅れて。
examplePolite.english: Sorry to keep you waiting. My train was late.

items.notes: Also said when handing over something people were waiting for, like food you cooked.

items.english: I'll be waiting; I'll wait for you
items.use: Said to someone on their way, or warmly at a goodbye to mean see you then.

example.romaji: wakatta. jaa, kafe de matteru ne.
example.ja: わかった。じゃあ、カフェで待ってるね。
example.english: Okay. I'll wait for you at the café, then.

examplePolite.romaji: wakarimashita. robii de matte imasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: わかりました。ロビーで待っていますね。
examplePolite.english: Understood. I'll be waiting in the lobby.

items.notes: To customers or seniors, omachi shite imasu is the humble version.

items.use: Said as you arrive late; the usual answer is ii yo or daijoubu.

example.romaji: okurete gomen! densha ga tomatteta n da.
example.ja: 遅れてごめん！電車が止まってたんだ。
example.english: Sorry I'm late! The train was stopped.

examplePolite.romaji: okurete sumimasen. michi ni mayotte shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 遅れてすみません。道に迷ってしまいました。
examplePolite.english: Sorry I'm late. I got lost.

items.notes: At work, okurete moushiwake arimasen is the stronger apology.

items.use: Texted or said before you arrive, usually with gomen and how long.

example.romaji: gomen, chotto okureru. juppun gurai.
example.ja: ごめん、ちょっと遅れる。10分ぐらい。
example.english: Sorry, I'll be a bit late. About ten minutes.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, densha ga okurete ite, sukoshi okuremasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、電車が遅れていて、少し遅れます。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, my train's delayed, so I'll be a little late.

items.notes: Okureru is also used for trains: densha ga okureteru (the train's late).

items.english: did you wait long?; have you been waiting?
items.use: Asked when you meet someone who got there first; the classic answer is uun, ima kita tokoro (no, I just got here).

example.romaji: gomen, matta? uun, ima kita tokoro.
example.ja: ごめん、待った？ううん、今来たところ。
example.english: Sorry, did you wait long? No, I just got here.

items.notes: Shouted, matta! means hold on! or wait!

blocks.label: Are you okay
blocks.rationale: Lets you check on someone who is hurt, upset or getting better.
blocks.interference: Daijoubu desu as an answer can mean no thanks, not just I'm fine.

items.english: are you all right?; are you okay?
items.use: Said to a stranger or someone older who fell, looks unwell or seems lost; with friends just daijoubu?

example.romaji: a, daijoubu desu ka? tatemasu ka?
example.ja: あ、大丈夫ですか？立てますか？
example.english: Oh, are you all right? Can you stand?

items.notes: Daijoubu desu as an answer often means no thanks, as when you're offered a bag.

items.english: did something happen?; is something wrong?
items.use: Asked when someone looks upset or calls out of the blue.

example.romaji: genki nai ne. nanika atta?
example.ja: 元気ないね。何かあった？
example.english: You seem down. Did something happen?

examplePolite.romaji: kaoiro ga warui desu yo. nanika atta n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 顔色が悪いですよ。何かあったんですか？
examplePolite.english: You look pale. Did something happen?

items.notes: Nanika atta no? is the softer, more caring version; dou shita no? (what's wrong?) is close.

items.use: Asked right after someone falls or there's an accident.
items.politeJa: お怪我はありませんか

example.romaji: abunakatta! daijoubu? kega nai?
example.ja: 危なかった！大丈夫？ケガない？
example.english: That was close! Are you okay? Are you hurt?

examplePolite.romaji: daijoubu desu ka? okega wa arimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: 大丈夫ですか？お怪我はありませんか？
examplePolite.english: Are you all right? Are you hurt?

items.notes: Kega means injury; kega shita means I got hurt.

items.english: are you feeling better now?; are you okay now?
items.use: Asked after someone was sick, hurt or upset; the answer is un, mou daijoubu.

example.romaji: kaze, mou daijoubu? kinou tsurasou datta kedo.
example.ja: 風邪、もう大丈夫？昨日つらそうだったけど。
example.english: Is your cold better? You looked rough yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: ashi wa mou daijoubu desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 足はもう大丈夫ですか？
examplePolite.english: Is your leg okay now?

items.notes: As a statement, mou daijoubu means it's all right now, said to calm someone.

blocks.label: Don't worry
blocks.rationale: Lets you reassure someone who apologizes, worries or rushes.
blocks.interference: Ki ni shinaide (don't mind it) and shinpai shinaide (don't be anxious) are not interchangeable.

items.english: don't worry about it; never mind
items.use: Said when someone apologizes or thanks you a lot, or feels bad about a mistake.
items.politeJa: 気にしないでください

example.romaji: ii yo, ki ni shinaide. dare demo machigaeru yo.
example.ja: いいよ、気にしないで。誰でも間違えるよ。
example.english: It's fine, don't worry about it. Everyone makes mistakes.

examplePolite.romaji: iie, ki ni shinaide kudasai. daijoubu desu.
examplePolite.ja: いいえ、気にしないでください。大丈夫です。
examplePolite.english: No, please don't worry about it. It's fine.

items.notes: Ki ni suru means mind or be bothered by; shinpai shinaide is about being anxious, not about minding.

items.use: Said to reassure someone about you or about a situation.
items.politeJa: 心配しないでください

example.romaji: daijoubu, shinpai shinaide. sugu kaeru kara.
example.ja: 大丈夫、心配しないで。すぐ帰るから。
example.english: I'm fine, don't worry. I'll be home soon.

examplePolite.romaji: shinpai shinaide kudasai. mou genki desu.
examplePolite.ja: 心配しないでください。もう元気です。
examplePolite.english: Please don't worry. I'm fine now.

items.notes: Shinpai kakete gomen means sorry I made you worry.

items.english: it'll work out; it'll be fine somehow
items.use: Said to calm someone stressed about a problem, or to yourself.

example.romaji: sonna ni shinpai shinakute mo, nantoka naru yo.
example.ja: そんなに心配しなくても、なんとかなるよ。
example.english: No need to worry so much. It'll work out.

examplePolite.romaji: daijoubu desu yo. kitto nantoka narimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 大丈夫ですよ。きっとなんとかなりますよ。
examplePolite.english: It's okay. I'm sure it'll work out.

items.notes: Nantoka suru means manage somehow: nantoka shite! (do something!).

items.use: Said to someone hurrying for your sake; people often say it when you're searching for words.
items.politeJa: ゆっくりでいいですよ

example.romaji: isoganakute ii kara, yukkuri de ii yo.
example.ja: 急がなくていいから、ゆっくりでいいよ。
example.english: You don't have to hurry. Take your time.

examplePolite.romaji: daijoubu desu yo, yukkuri de ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 大丈夫ですよ、ゆっくりでいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: It's all right, take your time.

items.notes: To ask someone to slow down: mou sukoshi yukkuri hanashite kudasai.

items.english: don't worry (about me); no need to worry
items.use: A polite way to turn down someone's concern or offer of help, often with people you don't know well.

example.romaji: hitori de kaeremasu kara, goshinpai naku.
example.ja: 一人で帰れますから、ご心配なく。
example.english: I can get home on my own, so don't worry.

items.notes: It can sound a bit cool, like I've got this; shinpai shinaide is warmer.

blocks.label: Yes, I did it
blocks.rationale: Cheer when you succeed or get lucky.
blocks.interference: yatta is your own win; yatta ne cheers someone else's.

items.use: Shouted when something good happens to you or you pull something off.

example.romaji: yatta! shiken ni ukatta yo!
example.ja: やった！試験に受かったよ！
example.english: Yes! I passed the exam!

examplePolite.romaji: yatta! shiken ni ukarimashita!
examplePolite.ja: やった！試験に受かりました！
examplePolite.english: Yes! I passed the exam!

items.notes: It's the past of yaru (do), but as a shout it just means joy. To cheer someone else, say yatta ne.

items.english: done; I did it; it's ready
items.use: Said when you finish making or managing something, often while showing it.

example.romaji: dekita! mite, kore jibun de tsukutta.
example.ja: できた！見て、これ自分で作った。
example.english: Done! Look, I made this myself.

examplePolite.romaji: dekimashita. mite kudasai, jibun de tsukurimashita.
examplePolite.ja: できました。見てください、自分で作りました。
examplePolite.english: Done. Have a look, I made it myself.

items.notes: Also 'it's ready' for food: gohan dekita yo (dinner's ready).

items.use: Said to yourself before starting something, or when something turns out well.

example.romaji: yoshi, ja hajimeyou ka.
example.ja: よし、じゃ始めようか。
example.english: Right, let's get started.

examplePolite.romaji: yoshi, sore dewa hajimemashou.
examplePolite.ja: よし、それでは始めましょう。
examplePolite.english: Right, let's begin then.

items.notes: Doubled, yoshi yoshi soothes or praises a child or pet.

items.use: Said when something goes your way by chance.

example.romaji: rakkii! saigo no hitotsu datta.
example.ja: ラッキー！最後の一つだった。
example.english: Lucky! It was the last one.

examplePolite.romaji: rakkii deshita. saigo no hitotsu deshita yo.
examplePolite.ja: ラッキーでした。最後の一つでしたよ。
examplePolite.english: I got lucky. It was the last one.

items.use: A punchy shout when you win or something goes your way, like a fist pump.

example.romaji: yossha, kore de owari da!
example.ja: よっしゃ、これで終わりだ！
example.english: All right, that's it, done!

items.notes: Sounds a bit macho; yatta is the neutral choice.

blocks.label: It's fine, no problem
blocks.rationale: Reassure people that all is well.
blocks.interference: nan demo nai (it's nothing) vs nan demo ii (anything is fine).

items.use: Casual yes to a plan or request; with a rising tone it asks 'okay?'.

example.romaji: okkee, ja ashita kuji ne.
example.ja: オッケー、じゃ明日九時ね。
example.english: OK, nine tomorrow then.

examplePolite.romaji: okkee desu. ja, ashita kuji ni onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: オッケーです。じゃ、明日九時にお願いします。
examplePolite.english: OK. Nine tomorrow, then.

items.notes: okkee desu is fine with coworkers; to a boss or client say wakarimashita.

items.use: Reassures someone that something is fine or will work.

example.romaji: mondai nai yo, ashita de ii.
example.ja: 問題ないよ、明日でいい。
example.english: No problem, tomorrow's fine.

examplePolite.romaji: mondai arimasen. ashita de daijoubu desu.
examplePolite.ja: 問題ありません。明日で大丈夫です。
examplePolite.english: No problem. Tomorrow is fine.

items.notes: Not used for 'you're welcome'; for that say iie or ii yo.

items.use: Said when someone asks what's wrong or what you said, and you'd rather drop it.

example.romaji: e? a, nan demo nai. ki ni shinaide.
example.ja: え？あ、何でもない。気にしないで。
example.english: Huh? Oh, it's nothing. Don't worry.

examplePolite.romaji: a, nan demo arimasen. ki ni shinaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: あ、何でもありません。気にしないでください。
examplePolite.english: Oh, it's nothing. Please don't worry.

items.notes: Don't confuse with nan demo ii (anything is fine).

items.english: it's no big deal; nothing serious
items.use: Plays down a problem, an injury, or praise.
items.politeJa: 大したことありません

example.romaji: kega? taishita koto nai yo.
example.ja: けが？大したことないよ。
example.english: The injury? It's nothing serious.

examplePolite.romaji: taishita koto arimasen yo. daijoubu desu.
examplePolite.ja: 大したことありませんよ。大丈夫です。
examplePolite.english: It's nothing serious. I'm fine.

items.notes: About someone else's work it's a put-down: 'not that impressive'.

blocks.label: Oh right, so true
blocks.rationale: Agree, confirm, or show you just remembered something.
blocks.interference: a, sou da is remembering, not agreeing.

items.use: Said when you check and see that what someone told you is true.

example.romaji: a, honto da. ame futteru.
example.ja: あ、ほんとだ。雨降ってる。
example.english: Oh, you're right. It's raining.

examplePolite.romaji: a, hontou desu ne. ame ga futte imasu.
examplePolite.ja: あ、本当ですね。雨が降っています。
examplePolite.english: Oh, so it is. It's raining.

items.notes: hontou? (really?) asks; honto da confirms.

items.english: oh, right; oh, I just remembered
items.use: Said when something suddenly comes to mind, just before you bring it up.

example.romaji: a, sou da. kore, omiyage.
example.ja: あ、そうだ。これ、お土産。
example.english: Oh, right. This is a souvenir for you.

examplePolite.romaji: a, sou da. kore, omiyage desu.
examplePolite.ja: あ、そうだ。これ、お土産です。
examplePolite.english: Oh, right. Here's a souvenir for you.

items.notes: Not agreement: for 'that's right' say sou da ne or sou desu.

items.use: Young people's reply when a friend says exactly what you were thinking.

example.romaji: sore na. ano eiga, maji de nagakatta.
example.ja: それな。あの映画、マジで長かった。
example.english: So true. That movie was seriously long.

items.notes: Sounds young and online; sou da yo ne is the safe everyday version.

items.use: Confirms that someone's guess or statement is correct.

example.romaji: sou, sono toori. yoku wakatta ne.
example.ja: そう、そのとおり。よくわかったね。
example.english: Yes, exactly. Good, you got it.

examplePolite.romaji: hai, sono toori desu.
examplePolite.ja: はい、そのとおりです。
examplePolite.english: Yes, that's exactly right.

items.notes: Sounds a bit firm, like a teacher; in chat sou sou or sou da yo is more common.

blocks.label: What is that
blocks.rationale: React when something surprises you or catches your eye.
blocks.interference: nani kore is about things near you, nani sore near the other person.

items.english: what's that?!; what's that supposed to mean
items.use: Reacts to something surprising the other person shows or says; your tone shows if you're curious or annoyed.

example.romaji: nani sore, kawaii! doko de katta no?
example.ja: 何それ、かわいい！どこで買ったの？
example.english: What's that? So cute! Where'd you buy it?

examplePolite.romaji: sore, nan desu ka? kawaii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: それ、何ですか？かわいいですね。
examplePolite.english: What's that? It's cute.

items.notes: Said flatly, it means 'that's ridiculous'.

items.use: Reacts to something right in front of you, in surprise, delight, or disgust.

example.romaji: nani kore, sugoku oishii!
example.ja: 何これ、すごくおいしい！
example.english: What is this? It's so good!

examplePolite.romaji: kore, nan desu ka? sugoku oishii desu.
examplePolite.ja: これ、何ですか？すごくおいしいです。
examplePolite.english: What is this? It's really good.

items.notes: kore is near you; sore is near the other person.

items.use: Shocked reaction to news; with a sharp tone it challenges what someone just said.

example.romaji: nan datte? kekkon suru no?
example.ja: なんだって？結婚するの？
example.english: What?! You're getting married?

items.notes: Asked calmly, it asks what someone else said: sensei, nan datte? (what did the teacher say?)

items.use: Said in shock or annoyance when you catch someone doing something odd or wrong.

example.romaji: chotto, nani yatten no! abunai yo.
example.ja: ちょっと、何やってんの！危ないよ。
example.english: Hey, what are you doing?! That's dangerous.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto, nani yatteru n desu ka! abunai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと、何やってるんですか！危ないですよ。
examplePolite.english: Hey, what are you doing? That's dangerous.

items.notes: For a neutral 'what are you up to?', ask nani shiteru no?

items.use: Eager reaction when you overhear something interesting and want in.

example.romaji: nani nani? nan no hanashi?
example.ja: なになに？何の話？
example.english: What, what? What are you talking about?

blocks.label: Really, no way
blocks.rationale: Show disbelief at surprising news.
blocks.interference: uso desho doesn't call anyone a liar.

items.use: For shocking news, good or bad.

example.romaji: uso, shinjirarenai! takarakuji atatta no?
example.ja: うそ、信じられない！宝くじ当たったの？
example.english: No way, I can't believe it! You won the lottery?

examplePolite.romaji: shinjiraremasen. takarakuji ga atatta n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 信じられません。宝くじが当たったんですか？
examplePolite.english: I can't believe it. You won the lottery?

items.notes: Said with a frown it scolds, like 'how could you?'.

items.use: Casual reaction to surprising news, often muttered to yourself.

example.romaji: maji ka, mou urikire?
example.ja: マジか、もう売り切れ？
example.english: Seriously? Sold out already?

items.notes: maji de? asks 'for real?'; politely say hontou desu ka.

items.english: no way; that's impossible; that's outrageous
items.use: Reacts to something hard to believe or hard to accept.

example.romaji: kyuuryou ga sagaru no? arienai!
example.ja: 給料が下がるの？ありえない！
example.english: Our pay's going down? That's outrageous!

examplePolite.romaji: kyuuryou ga sagaru n desu ka? arienai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 給料が下がるんですか？ありえないです。
examplePolite.english: Our pay's going down? That's unbelievable.

items.notes: Young people also use it as praise: arienai kurai oishii (unbelievably good).

items.use: Disbelief at news you don't want to be true.

example.romaji: uso desho? mou owari?
example.ja: うそでしょ？もう終わり？
example.english: You're kidding. It's over already?

items.notes: It doesn't call anyone a liar; politely, say hontou desu ka.

blocks.label: Oh no, what now
blocks.rationale: React when something goes wrong.
blocks.interference: shimatta is about your mistake; dou shiyou is not knowing what to do next.

items.use: Said when you realize you've made a mistake or forgotten something.

example.romaji: shimatta, saifu ie ni wasureta.
example.ja: しまった、財布家に忘れた。
example.english: Oh no, I left my wallet at home.

examplePolite.romaji: a, shimatta. saifu o ie ni wasuremashita.
examplePolite.ja: あ、しまった。財布を家に忘れました。
examplePolite.english: Oh no. I left my wallet at home.

items.notes: For your own slip-ups; yabai is the more casual everyday version.

items.english: what do I do?; oh no
items.use: Panicky self-talk when you're in trouble and don't know what to do.

example.romaji: dou shiyou, kagi nakushita.
example.ja: どうしよう、鍵なくした。
example.english: What do I do? I lost my keys.

examplePolite.romaji: dou shimashou, kagi o nakushite shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: どうしましょう、鍵をなくしてしまいました。
examplePolite.english: What should I do? I've lost my keys.

items.notes: Asked calmly, dou shiyou ka? just means 'what shall we do?' when planning.

items.use: A quick reflex when you nearly drop, bump into, or let slip something.

example.romaji: otto, abunai. ki o tsukete.
example.ja: おっと、危ない。気をつけて。
example.english: Whoa, careful. Watch out.

examplePolite.romaji: otto, sumimasen, shitsurei shimashita.
examplePolite.ja: おっと、すみません、失礼しました。
examplePolite.english: Oops, sorry, excuse me.

items.use: Puzzled self-talk when something isn't where or how it should be.

example.romaji: okashii na, koko ni oita no ni.
example.ja: おかしいな、ここに置いたのに。
example.english: That's strange, I put it right here.

examplePolite.romaji: okashii desu ne, koko ni oita n desu ga.
examplePolite.ja: おかしいですね、ここに置いたんですが。
examplePolite.english: That's odd, I put it right here.

items.notes: okashii also means funny: okashii hanashi (a funny story).

blocks.label: Got it or not
blocks.rationale: Tell someone you understood, or that you didn't.
blocks.interference: wakarimashita and wakarimasen differ only in the ending, so listen for -shita versus -sen.

items.use: Polite reply when someone explains something or asks you to do something; with friends, say wakatta.

example.romaji: hai, wakarimashita. ashita made ni yarimasu.
example.ja: はい、わかりました。明日までにやります。
example.english: Okay, understood. I'll have it done by tomorrow.

items.notes: To a boss or customer, shouchi shimashita or kashikomarimashita sounds more formal.

items.english: I don't understand; I don't know
items.use: Polite way to say you don't follow or can't answer; with friends, say wakannai.

example.romaji: sumimasen, nihongo ga yoku wakarimasen.
example.ja: すみません、日本語がよくわかりません。
example.english: Sorry, I don't really understand Japanese.

items.notes: For facts, shirimasen also means 'I don't know' but can sound cold; wakarimasen is softer.

items.use: A cheerful drawn-out yes, called back when someone calls your name or asks you to do something; shop staff use it too.

example.romaji: haai, ima iku kara chotto matte!
example.ja: はーい、今行くからちょっと待って！
example.english: Coming! Just a sec!

examplePolite.romaji: haai, ima sugu ikimasu!
examplePolite.ja: はーい、今すぐ行きます！
examplePolite.english: Coming, right away!

items.notes: A short hai is the plain yes; haai sounds friendly, or childish if overused.

items.use: Quick okay to a plan or instruction, very common in texts between friends and coworkers.

example.romaji: ryoukai, ja eki de matteru ne.
example.ja: 了解、じゃ駅で待ってるね。
example.english: Got it, I'll wait at the station then.

examplePolite.romaji: ryoukai shimashita. eki de matte imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 了解しました。駅で待っています。
examplePolite.english: Understood. I'll wait at the station.

items.notes: Some people find ryoukai shimashita too blunt for a boss; shouchi shimashita is safer upward.

blocks.label: When you didn't catch it
blocks.rationale: Get people to repeat or slow down, and handle the compliment learners always get.
blocks.interference: kikoenakatta is about hearing; wakarimasen is about understanding.

items.english: once more, please; could you say that again?
items.use: Ask someone to repeat what they said; staff and teachers hear it from learners all the time.
items.ja: もう一度お願いします
items.kana: もういちどおねがいします

example.romaji: sumimasen, mou ichido onegai shimasu.
example.ja: すみません、もう一度お願いします。
example.english: Sorry, could you say that again?

items.notes: Casual: mou ikkai itte. Add yukkuri (slowly) if speed is the problem.

items.english: I didn't catch that; I couldn't hear
items.use: When noise or a quiet voice is the problem; usually followed by a request to repeat.

example.romaji: gomen, kikoenakatta. mou ikkai itte?
example.ja: ごめん、聞こえなかった。もう一回言って？
example.english: Sorry, I didn't catch that. Say it again?

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, kikoemasen deshita. mou ichido onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、聞こえませんでした。もう一度お願いします。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I couldn't hear. Once more, please.

items.notes: kikoeru is 'can be heard'; kiku is 'listen' or 'ask'.

items.use: Ask a fast speaker to slow down; mou sukoshi (a bit more) makes it softer.
items.ja: ゆっくり話してください
items.kana: ゆっくりはなしてください

example.romaji: sumimasen, mou sukoshi yukkuri hanashite kudasai.
example.ja: すみません、もう少しゆっくり話してください。
example.english: Sorry, could you speak a little more slowly?

items.notes: With friends, just yukkuri itte.

items.use: Said to learners, often after only a few words; answer iie, mada mada desu (no, I've a long way to go).
items.kana: にほんごじょうずですね

example.romaji: e, nihongo jouzu desu ne! doko de benkyou shita n desu ka?
example.ja: え、日本語上手ですね！どこで勉強したんですか？
example.english: Oh, your Japanese is good! Where did you learn?

items.notes: Usually politeness, not a real assessment. Friends say nihongo umai ne.

blocks.label: Agreeing strongly
blocks.rationale: Say 'yes, exactly' and 'I know the feeling', with friends or to a boss.
blocks.interference: wakaru wakaru means 'I feel the same', not 'I understand'.

items.use: Eager agreement when someone says what you were thinking; also opens something you just remembered.

example.romaji: sou sou, sore ga iitakatta no!
example.ja: そうそう、それが言いたかったの！
example.english: Yes, exactly, that's what I was trying to say!

examplePolite.romaji: sou sou, sore ga iitakatta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: そうそう、それが言いたかったんです。
examplePolite.english: Yes, exactly, that's what I was trying to say.

items.notes: A single sou desu ne is calmer agreement.

items.english: I know, I know; I totally get it
items.use: Sympathy when a friend describes a feeling or situation you've had too.

example.romaji: wakaru wakaru, getsuyoubi tte honto ni darui yo ne.
example.ja: わかるわかる、月曜日ってほんとにだるいよね。
example.english: I know, right? Mondays are such a drag.

items.notes: It means 'I feel the same', not 'I understand your words'.

items.english: you're quite right; exactly as you say
items.use: Respectful agreement to a boss, client or customer, often before an apology or a fix.
items.ja: おっしゃるとおりです
items.kana: おっしゃるとおりです

example.romaji: ossharu toori desu. sugu ni naoshimasu.
example.ja: おっしゃるとおりです。すぐに直します。
example.english: You're quite right. I'll fix it right away.

items.notes: ossharu is the respectful form of iu (say). Among friends, sono toori is enough.

blocks.label: Tired or fine
blocks.rationale: Say how you feel and how you slept.
blocks.interference: yoku neta uses neru (sleep); nemurenakatta uses nemureru (can sleep).

items.use: Past tense because it describes how you feel now; often a sigh at the end of the day.

example.romaji: aa, tsukareta. kyou wa hayaku neyou.
example.ja: ああ、疲れた。今日は早く寝よう。
example.english: Ugh, I'm tired. I'm going to bed early tonight.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa chotto tsukaremashita. hayaku nemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はちょっと疲れました。早く寝ます。
examplePolite.english: I'm a bit tired today. I'll go to bed early.

items.notes: Related: otsukare, the 'good work' greeting at the end of a job or day.

items.english: totally fine; no problem at all
items.use: Reassure someone who apologizes or asks if you're okay.
items.kana: ぜんぜんだいじょうぶ

example.romaji: un, zenzen daijoubu da yo. ki ni shinaide.
example.ja: うん、全然大丈夫だよ。気にしないで。
example.english: Yeah, totally fine. Don't worry about it.

examplePolite.romaji: hai, zenzen daijoubu desu. ki ni shinaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: はい、全然大丈夫です。気にしないでください。
examplePolite.english: Yes, totally fine. Please don't worry about it.

items.notes: Textbooks say zenzen needs a negative, but zenzen daijoubu is normal everyday speech.

items.use: Said on waking with a stretch, or as the answer to yoku neta? (did you sleep well?).

example.romaji: un, yuube wa yoku neta yo. arigatou.
example.ja: うん、ゆうべはよく寝たよ。ありがとう。
example.english: Yeah, I slept well last night, thanks.

examplePolite.romaji: hai, okagesama de yuube wa yoku nemashita.
examplePolite.ja: はい、おかげさまでゆうべはよく寝ました。
examplePolite.english: Yes, thanks, I slept well last night.

items.notes: Politely, people also ask and answer with yoku nemuremashita (were able to sleep well).

items.use: Explains why you're tired or out of it today.

example.romaji: kinou zenzen nemurenakatta. ima sugoku nemui.
example.ja: 昨日全然眠れなかった。今すごく眠い。
example.english: I couldn't sleep at all last night. I'm so sleepy now.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou wa amari nemuremasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日はあまり眠れませんでした。
examplePolite.english: I didn't sleep very well last night.

items.notes: nerarenakatta means the same and is just as common.

blocks.label: Hungry, thirsty, full
blocks.rationale: Say you're hungry, thirsty, full or drunk.
blocks.interference: hara hetta is rough; onaka pekopeko works for anyone.

items.use: Blunt everyday way to say you're hungry, mostly among male friends and family.

example.romaji: aa, hara hetta. nanka tabe ni ikou.
example.ja: ああ、腹減った。なんか食べに行こう。
example.english: Man, I'm starving. Let's go grab something.

items.notes: Neutral: onaka suita. Polite: onaka ga sukimashita.

items.use: Say when you can't eat any more, or to turn down seconds.

example.romaji: mou onaka ippai, taberarenai.
example.ja: もうお腹いっぱい、食べられない。
example.english: I'm full, I can't eat another bite.

examplePolite.romaji: mou onaka ippai desu. gochisousama deshita.
examplePolite.ja: もうお腹いっぱいです。ごちそうさまでした。
examplePolite.english: I'm full. Thank you for the meal.

items.notes: Also figurative: 'I've had enough of that'.

items.use: Literally 'my throat has dried'; the everyday way to say you want a drink.

example.romaji: nodo kawaita, nanka nomou yo.
example.ja: 喉渇いた、なんか飲もうよ。
example.english: I'm thirsty, let's get a drink.

examplePolite.romaji: nodo ga kawakimashita ne. nanika nomimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: 喉が渇きましたね。何か飲みませんか？
examplePolite.english: I'm thirsty. Shall we get something to drink?

items.notes: Past tense because it describes the state now, like tsukareta.

items.use: Soft, cute way to say you're very hungry; fine for anyone, common with kids.

example.romaji: mou onaka pekopeko, hayaku tabeyou!
example.ja: もうお腹ペコペコ、早く食べよう！
example.english: I'm starving, let's eat already!

examplePolite.romaji: mou onaka pekopeko desu. hayaku tabemashou.
examplePolite.ja: もうお腹ペコペコです。早く食べましょう。
examplePolite.english: I'm starving. Let's eat soon.

items.notes: Gentler than hara hetta; pekopeko is the sound-word for an empty stomach.

items.use: Say you've had too much; chotto yopparatta is 'I'm a bit tipsy'.

example.romaji: chotto yopparatta kamo. mizu choudai.
example.ja: ちょっと酔っ払ったかも。水ちょうだい。
example.english: I might be a bit drunk. Can I have some water?

examplePolite.romaji: chotto yopparatte shimaimashita. omizu o kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと酔っ払ってしまいました。お水をください。
examplePolite.english: I've had a bit too much. Could I have some water?

items.notes: yotta is a milder 'tipsy', and also means carsick or seasick.

blocks.label: How was it
blocks.rationale: Ask how something went and say it was fun or good.
blocks.interference: tanoshikatta is for fun you had; omoshirokatta is for something interesting or funny.

items.english: that was fun; I had a great time
items.use: Say after a trip, party or day out; the usual answer to dou datta?

example.romaji: kyou wa honto ni tanoshikatta! mata ikou ne.
example.ja: 今日はほんとに楽しかった！また行こうね。
example.english: Today was so much fun! Let's go again.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa hontou ni tanoshikatta desu. mata ikimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は本当に楽しかったです。また行きましょう。
examplePolite.english: I really enjoyed today. Let's go again.

items.notes: For a funny or interesting film or book, omoshirokatta fits better.

items.use: Ask about a trip, test, date or meal that's over; answer tanoshikatta, yokatta, or maa maa (so-so).

example.romaji: ryokou dou datta? tanoshikatta?
example.ja: 旅行どうだった？楽しかった？
example.english: How was the trip? Was it fun?

examplePolite.romaji: ryokou wa dou deshita ka? tanoshikatta desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 旅行はどうでしたか？楽しかったですか？
examplePolite.english: How was your trip? Did you enjoy it?

items.notes: dou desu ka asks about now; dou datta asks about something finished.

items.english: what's it like?; how's it going?
items.use: Ask for a quick impression of a place or thing, or how something is going; answer ii kanji (going well).

example.romaji: atarashii shigoto, donna kanji?
example.ja: 新しい仕事、どんな感じ？
example.english: How's the new job going?

examplePolite.romaji: atarashii oshigoto, donna kanji desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 新しいお仕事、どんな感じですか？
examplePolite.english: How's your new job going?

items.notes: kanji here is 'feel', not the Chinese characters.

items.english: that was interesting; that was fun; that was funny
items.use: For films, books, talks or anything that held your interest or made you laugh.

example.romaji: ano eiga, sugoku omoshirokatta yo.
example.ja: あの映画、すごく面白かったよ。
example.english: That movie was really good.

examplePolite.romaji: ano eiga, sugoku omoshirokatta desu.
examplePolite.ja: あの映画、すごく面白かったです。
examplePolite.english: That movie was really good.

items.notes: omoshiroi is 'interesting' as much as 'funny'; for a fun event, tanoshikatta fits better.

blocks.label: Catching up with friends
blocks.rationale: Lets you ask how someone has been and react when you meet again.
blocks.interference: Genki datta? needs a gap since you last met; saikin dou? works for people you see often.

items.use: To someone you haven't seen for a while; answer un, genki datta yo, or with your news.

example.romaji: uwa, hisashiburi! genki datta?
example.ja: うわ、久しぶり！元気だった？
example.english: Wow, long time no see! How've you been?

examplePolite.romaji: ohisashiburi desu. ogenki deshita ka?
examplePolite.ja: お久しぶりです。お元気でしたか？
examplePolite.english: It's been a long time. How have you been?

items.notes: Only after a gap; for someone you saw last week, use saikin dou?

items.use: Opens a catch-up with a friend or coworker; answer with a bit of news, or maa maa (so-so).

example.romaji: saikin dou? shigoto isogashii?
example.ja: 最近どう？仕事忙しい？
example.english: How's it going? Busy with work?

examplePolite.romaji: saikin dou desu ka? oshigoto wa isogashii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 最近どうですか？お仕事は忙しいですか？
examplePolite.english: How have things been? Is work busy?

items.notes: The closest thing to English 'how are you?' for people you see often.

items.english: how are they doing?; what are you up to these days?
items.use: Asks about someone's life now, often about a person who isn't there.

example.romaji: sotsugyou shite kara, minna dou shiteru?
example.ja: 卒業してから、みんなどうしてる？
example.english: How's everyone been since graduation?

examplePolite.romaji: sotsugyou shite kara, minasan dou shite imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 卒業してから、皆さんどうしていますか？
examplePolite.english: How is everyone doing since graduation?

items.notes: Often with kana: ima dou shiteru kana (I wonder how they're doing).

items.english: no change; all well, same as ever
items.use: As a question it asks if all is well since you last met; as an answer it means nothing new, all fine.
items.politeJa: お変わりありませんか

example.romaji: hisashiburi da ne. kawari nai?
example.ja: 久しぶりだね。変わりない？
example.english: Long time no see. All good?

examplePolite.romaji: ohisashiburi desu. okawari arimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: お久しぶりです。お変わりありませんか？
examplePolite.english: It's been a while. Is everything well with you?

items.notes: A common answer is un, aikawarazu (yeah, same as ever).

items.use: Said at a reunion, usually as a warm compliment; also about a place.

example.romaji: uwa, zenzen kawatte nai ne!
example.ja: うわ、全然変わってないね！
example.english: Wow, you haven't changed at all!

examplePolite.romaji: sensei, zenzen kawatte imasen ne!
examplePolite.ja: 先生、全然変わっていませんね！
examplePolite.english: You haven't changed at all, sensei!

items.notes: Can also tease: still the same old you.

blocks.label: See you again
blocks.rationale: Lets you say when you'll meet next.
blocks.interference: Mata kondo is often a polite no, not a real plan.

items.use: When you'll meet or talk again the same day.

example.romaji: ima isogashii kara, mata ato de ne.
example.ja: 今忙しいから、また後でね。
example.english: I'm busy right now, so later, okay?

examplePolite.romaji: mata nochihodo renraku shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: また後ほど連絡します。
examplePolite.english: I'll get back to you later.

items.notes: Not for 'see you someday'; that's mata kondo or mata ne.

items.use: Puts a plan off to some later time; also the soft way to turn down an invitation.

example.romaji: kyou wa muri da kedo, mata kondo ne.
example.ja: 今日は無理だけど、また今度ね。
example.english: I can't today, but next time.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa chotto... mata kondo onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はちょっと…また今度お願いします。
examplePolite.english: Today's a bit... maybe another time.

items.notes: Often a polite no: don't expect a date to follow.

items.use: Goodbye to people you see weekly: classmates, a teacher, coworkers on a Friday.

example.romaji: otsukare! mata raishuu ne.
example.ja: お疲れ！また来週ね。
example.english: Good work! See you next week.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou mo arigatou gozaimashita. mata raishuu yoroshiku onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日もありがとうございました。また来週よろしくお願いします。
examplePolite.english: Thanks again for today. See you next week.

items.use: A warm goodbye between friends after spending time together.

example.romaji: kyou tanoshikatta! mata asobou ne.
example.ja: 今日楽しかった！また遊ぼうね。
example.english: Today was fun! Let's hang out again.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa tanoshikatta desu. mata asobimashou ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は楽しかったです。また遊びましょうね。
examplePolite.english: Today was fun. Let's get together again.

items.notes: Asobu covers adults hanging out, not just kids playing.

blocks.label: Time to go
blocks.rationale: Lets you wrap up a visit or leave work before others.
blocks.interference: Osaki ni also starts osaki ni douzo (after you); the situation decides.

items.use: Signals you're about to leave a visit, a cafe or a party; the 'go home' part is left unsaid.

example.romaji: jaa sorosoro. ashita hayai shi.
example.ja: じゃあそろそろ。明日早いし。
example.english: Well, I should go. I've got an early start.

examplePolite.romaji: dewa sorosoro shitsurei shimasu. gochisousama deshita.
examplePolite.ja: ではそろそろ失礼します。ごちそうさまでした。
examplePolite.english: Well, I'll be going. Thank you for the meal.

items.notes: Sorosoro alone means 'about time' or 'soon'.

items.use: Suggests to the group that it's time to leave, or to move on to the next place.
items.politeJa: そろそろ行きましょうか

example.romaji: mou juuji da. sorosoro ikou ka.
example.ja: もう十時だ。そろそろ行こうか。
example.english: It's already ten. Shall we get going?

examplePolite.romaji: mou juuji desu ne. sorosoro ikimashou ka.
examplePolite.ja: もう十時ですね。そろそろ行きましょうか。
examplePolite.english: It's already ten. Shall we get going?

items.notes: Swap the verb: sorosoro kaerou ka (shall we head home?).

items.english: I'm heading off (before you); after you
items.use: Short form for leaving before others, or with douzo for letting someone go first.

example.romaji: jaa, osaki ni! otsukare.
example.ja: じゃあ、お先に！お疲れ。
example.english: Okay, I'm heading off! Good work.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, osaki ni shitsurei shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、お先に失礼します。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I'll be leaving before you.

items.notes: Also before eating or bathing first: osaki ni itadakimasu.

items.english: I'll be leaving now, before you
items.use: Said to coworkers still working when you leave; they answer otsukaresama deshita.
items.kana: おさきにしつれいします

example.romaji: kyou wa kore de, osaki ni shitsurei shimasu.
example.ja: 今日はこれで、お先に失礼します。
example.english: That's it for me today. I'll head off before you.

items.notes: Also for leaving a party or meeting early.

blocks.label: Take care on parting
blocks.rationale: Lets you send someone off warmly and pass on greetings.
blocks.interference: Genki de ne implies a long parting; for an ordinary night say ki o tsukete kaette ne.

items.use: Said to someone heading home, especially at night or in bad weather; answer un, arigatou.
items.kana: きをつけてかえってね
items.politeJa: 気をつけてお帰りください

example.romaji: mou kurai kara, ki o tsukete kaette ne.
example.ja: もう暗いから、気をつけて帰ってね。
example.english: It's dark now, so get home safe.

examplePolite.romaji: ame ga tsuyoi node, ki o tsukete okaeri kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 雨が強いので、気をつけてお帰りください。
examplePolite.english: It's raining hard, so get home safely.

items.notes: Ki o tsukete alone means take care, or watch out.

items.use: Polite send-off to someone leaving: a guest, a customer, a coworker going on a trip.

example.romaji: kyou wa arigatou gozaimashita. oki o tsukete.
example.ja: 今日はありがとうございました。お気をつけて。
example.english: Thank you for today. Take care.

items.notes: Casual form: ki o tsukete.

items.use: Said when you won't see someone for a long time, like before a move or at the end of a trip.

example.romaji: mukou de mo genki de ne.
example.ja: 向こうでも元気でね。
