example.english: Take care of yourself over there.

examplePolite.romaji: atarashii shigoto, ganbatte kudasai. ogenki de.
examplePolite.ja: 新しい仕事、頑張ってください。お元気で。
examplePolite.english: Good luck with the new job. Take care.

items.notes: Not for an ordinary daily goodbye; it implies a long time apart.

items.english: say hi to them for me
items.use: Sends your regards to someone who isn't there, usually as you part: X ni yoroshiku tsutaete.
items.politeJa: よろしくお伝えください

example.romaji: okaasan ni yoroshiku tsutaete ne.
example.ja: お母さんによろしく伝えてね。
example.english: Say hi to your mom for me.

examplePolite.romaji: okusan ni yoroshiku otsutae kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 奥さんによろしくお伝えください。
examplePolite.english: Please give my regards to your wife.

items.notes: Often cut to just X ni yoroshiku.

blocks.label: Small talk with neighbours
blocks.rationale: Lets you trade the weather and doorstep lines that open daily chats.
blocks.interference: Odekake desu ka isn't really asking where you're going.

items.use: The default summer opener with neighbours, shop staff or coworkers; agree with hontou ni, atsui desu ne.

example.romaji: kyou mo atsui desu ne. ase ga tomaranai desu.
example.ja: 今日も暑いですね。汗が止まらないです。
example.english: Hot again today, isn't it? I can't stop sweating.

items.notes: With friends: atsui ne. Hot food and baths are atsui too.

items.use: The winter version of atsui desu ne; an easy way to greet anyone.

example.romaji: kesa wa hontou ni samui desu ne.
example.ja: 今朝は本当に寒いですね。
example.english: It's really cold this morning, isn't it?

items.notes: With friends: samui ne. For cold drinks or water, use tsumetai, not samui.

items.use: Light opener with a neighbour or someone at a bus stop; agree with sou desu ne.

example.romaji: kyou wa ii tenki desu ne. osanpo desu ka?
example.ja: 今日はいい天気ですね。お散歩ですか？
example.english: Lovely day today. Out for a walk?

items.notes: With friends: ii tenki da ne.

items.use: A neighbour's greeting when they see you leaving; it isn't really asking where, so answer vaguely.

example.romaji: a, ohayou gozaimasu. odekake desu ka?
example.ja: あ、おはようございます。お出かけですか？
example.english: Oh, good morning. Off out?

items.notes: The stock answer is ee, chotto soko made (just up the road).

blocks.label: Thanks for real help
blocks.rationale: Lets you thank people for help over time or for getting you out of a fix.
blocks.interference: Osewa ni narimashita is for endings; the ongoing osewa ni natte imasu is a work greeting.

items.english: that really helped; you saved me
items.use: Thanks that stresses the relief someone gave you, like lending you something or covering for you.

example.romaji: kasa kashite kurete, hontou ni tasukatta yo.
example.ja: 傘貸してくれて、本当に助かったよ。
example.english: Thanks for lending me the umbrella, it really saved me.

examplePolite.romaji: kasa o kashite kudasatte, hontou ni tasukarimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 傘を貸してくださって、本当に助かりました。
examplePolite.english: Thank you for lending me the umbrella, it really helped.

items.notes: Also 'phew, saved' after a close call. Tasukaru (present) accepts an offer: sou shite kureru to tasukaru.

items.use: Thanks for help over a stretch of time, often when someone leaves or a trip ends.
items.politeJa: いろいろありがとうございました

example.romaji: kono isshuukan, iroiro arigatou ne.
example.ja: この一週間、いろいろありがとうね。
example.english: Thanks for everything this week.

examplePolite.romaji: kono isshuukan, iroiro arigatou gozaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: この一週間、いろいろありがとうございました。
examplePolite.english: Thank you for everything this week.

items.use: Thanks for continuing help: staff to regular customers, or you to a coworker or delivery driver you see often.
items.ja: いつもありがとうございます
items.kana: いつもありがとうございます

example.romaji: itsumo arigatou gozaimasu. kyou wa nan ni shimasu ka?
example.ja: いつもありがとうございます。今日は何にしますか？
example.english: Thanks for coming again. What'll it be today?

items.notes: To family or friends: itsumo arigatou ne.

items.english: thank you for all your help (at the end)
items.use: Said when a stay, job or course of care ends: to a host family, your old boss, hospital staff.

example.romaji: sannenkan, hontou ni osewa ni narimashita.
example.ja: 三年間、本当にお世話になりました。
example.english: Thank you so much for these three years.

items.notes: The ongoing form, osewa ni natte imasu, opens work emails and calls.

blocks.label: Work greetings
blocks.rationale: Lets you greet coworkers and thank people for their work.
blocks.interference: Gokurousama only goes to people below you or service staff; to bosses say otsukaresama.

items.english: hello; thanks for your hard work (between coworkers)
items.use: The all-purpose work greeting: passing a coworker, starting a call or message, coming back to the office.

example.romaji: otsukaresama desu. kaigi, mou hajimatte imasu ka?
example.ja: お疲れ様です。会議、もう始まっていますか？
example.english: Hi. Has the meeting started yet?

items.notes: Friends say otsukare after a club, a shift or a long day.

items.english: good work today; thanks for your hard work
items.use: Said when work or an event ends, especially to someone leaving; the answer to osaki ni shitsurei shimasu.

example.romaji: kyou wa nagai ichinichi deshita ne. otsukaresama deshita.
example.ja: 今日は長い一日でしたね。お疲れ様でした。
example.english: Long day today. Good work.

items.notes: Casual: otsukare. Also said after a match, a show or a long trip.

items.english: thanks for your trouble (to workers, juniors)
items.use: Said to delivery drivers, guards or juniors doing a job for you; not to your boss.

example.romaji: samui naka, gokurousama desu.
example.ja: 寒い中、ご苦労様です。
example.english: Thanks for coming out in the cold.

items.notes: Said upward it sounds bossy; to anyone above you, use otsukaresama desu.

items.english: thanks for your trouble; good job
items.use: Casual thanks from a boss or older person to someone below them; you'll mostly hear it.

example.romaji: kyou wa gokurousan. mou agatte ii yo.
example.ja: 今日はご苦労さん。もう上がっていいよ。
example.english: Thanks for today. You can head home now.

examplePolite.romaji: ame no naka, gokurousama desu.
examplePolite.ja: 雨の中、ご苦労様です。
examplePolite.english: Thanks for coming out in the rain.

items.notes: Only from higher to lower; never say it to your boss.

blocks.label: Welcoming a guest in
blocks.rationale: Lets you follow a host's welcome at the door and inside.
blocks.interference: Irasshai is a host's welcome; shop staff's irasshaimase needs no answer.

items.use: A host greets a visitor at the door, or a small shop owner greets customers; the guest answers ojama shimasu.

example.romaji: irasshai! samukatta deshou, haitte.
example.ja: いらっしゃい！寒かったでしょう、入って。
example.english: Welcome! You must be cold, come in.

examplePolite.romaji: irasshaimase. nanmeisama desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: いらっしゃいませ。何名様ですか？
examplePolite.english: Welcome. How many in your party?

items.notes: Shop staff's irasshaimase needs no reply; a nod is fine.

items.use: A host invites you up from the entryway into the house; take your shoes off and say ojama shimasu.

example.romaji: douzo, oagari kudasai. surippa, kochira desu.
example.ja: どうぞ、お上がりください。スリッパ、こちらです。
example.english: Please, come on in. Here are some slippers.

items.notes: Casual: agatte, agatte. Agaru is stepping up from the entryway.

items.use: A host tells a guest to sit however they like, often to someone kneeling formally.

example.romaji: ashi kuzushite, raku ni shite ne.
example.ja: 足崩して、楽にしてね。
example.english: Stretch your legs out, make yourself comfortable.

examplePolite.romaji: douzo oraku ni. ocha iremasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: どうぞお楽に。お茶入れますね。
examplePolite.english: Please, make yourself comfortable. I'll make some tea.

items.notes: Doctors say it too: raku ni shite kudasai (relax).

items.use: Staff, hosts or interviewers invite you to sit; say shitsurei shimasu as you sit down.

example.romaji: douzo, kochira ni okake kudasai.
example.ja: どうぞ、こちらにおかけください。
example.english: Please, have a seat here.

items.notes: Casual: suwatte. In waiting rooms you'll hear okake ni natte omachi kudasai.

blocks.label: Guest and host courtesies
blocks.rationale: Lets you enter and leave a home politely and handle offers of food.
blocks.interference: Ojama shimasu is arriving and ojama shimashita leaving; enryo shinaide is the host, enryo naku the guest's reply.

items.use: Said by a guest stepping into someone's home or office, or joining a group.

example.romaji: ojama shimasu. kore, minna de tabete kudasai.
example.ja: お邪魔します。これ、みんなで食べてください。
example.english: Thanks for having me. Here's something for everyone.

items.notes: Friends just say ojama. Plain jama means 'in the way', and jama da! is rude.

items.use: Said by a guest at the door when leaving someone's home; the host answers mata kite ne.

example.romaji: kyou wa ojama shimashita. tanoshikatta desu.
example.ja: 今日はお邪魔しました。楽しかったです。
example.english: Thanks for having me today. It was fun.

items.notes: The pair: ojama shimasu coming in, ojama shimashita going out.

items.use: A host or friend urging you to eat, sit or ask for something; accept with jaa, enryo naku.

example.romaji: takusan aru kara, enryo shinaide tabete.
example.ja: たくさんあるから、遠慮しないで食べて。
example.english: There's plenty, so don't be shy, eat up.

examplePolite.romaji: takusan arimasu kara, goenryo naku douzo.
examplePolite.ja: たくさんありますから、ご遠慮なくどうぞ。
examplePolite.english: There's plenty, so please help yourself.

items.notes: Enryo is holding back out of politeness; guests decline once, so hosts insist.

items.english: without holding back; I'll gladly take it
items.use: Said when accepting an offer after the host insists, or to urge someone: enryo naku itte (just tell me).
items.politeJa: 遠慮なくいただきます

example.romaji: jaa, enryo naku moratte iku ne.
example.ja: じゃあ、遠慮なくもらっていくね。
example.english: Well then, I'll gladly take it.

examplePolite.romaji: dewa, enryo naku itadakimasu.
examplePolite.ja: では、遠慮なくいただきます。
examplePolite.english: Well then, I'll gladly accept.

items.english: please don't go to any trouble
items.use: A guest's polite line when the host offers tea or food.

example.romaji: a, douzo okamai naku. sugu kaerimasu kara.
example.ja: あ、どうぞおかまいなく。すぐ帰りますから。
example.english: Oh, please don't trouble yourself. I'm leaving soon.

items.notes: The host usually brings tea anyway; just thank them.

blocks.label: Courtesy with strangers
blocks.rationale: Lets you make way, get off a packed train and excuse yourself politely.
blocks.interference: Shitsurei shimashita is sorry for a slip; shitsurei desu ga opens a question.

items.use: Letting someone go first at a door, lift or till; they answer sumimasen or doumo.

example.romaji: watashi wa ato de ii kara, osaki ni douzo.
example.ja: 私は後でいいから、お先にどうぞ。
example.english: I can go later, so go ahead.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi wa ato de daijoubu desu kara, osaki ni douzo.
examplePolite.ja: 私は後で大丈夫ですから、お先にどうぞ。
examplePolite.english: I'm fine going later, so please go ahead.

items.notes: A host may also offer you the bath first with it.

items.use: Light polite apology for a small slip: bumping someone, a wrong number, walking into the wrong room.

example.romaji: a, heya o machigaemashita. shitsurei shimashita.
example.ja: あ、部屋を間違えました。失礼しました。
example.english: Oh, wrong room. Excuse me.

items.notes: Shitsurei shimasu (present) is for entering, leaving or hanging up.

items.english: I'm getting off (on a crowded train or bus)
items.use: Said aloud to the people in your way as your stop comes, so they make room.

example.romaji: sumimasen, orimasu! chotto tooshite kudasai.
example.ja: すみません、降ります！ちょっと通してください。
example.english: Excuse me, getting off! Let me through, please.

items.notes: From oriru (get off). In a crowd, sumimasen alone also works.

items.use: Opens a personal or awkward question to someone you don't know well, like their name, age or company.

example.romaji: shitsurei desu ga, otoshi wa oikutsu desu ka?
example.ja: 失礼ですが、お年はおいくつですか？
example.english: Excuse me for asking, but how old are you?

items.notes: Not for getting someone's attention; use sumimasen for that.

blocks.label: Offering things and help
blocks.rationale: Lets you offer food, a turn or a hand without pressure.
blocks.interference: Ikaga desu ka offers politely; douzo douzo hands over or lets someone go first.

items.english: would you like some?; how about it?; how is it?
items.use: Polite offer or check-in from staff or a host (fukuro wa ikaga desu ka?); answer onegai shimasu or daijoubu desu.

example.romaji: koohii no okawari, ikaga desu ka?
example.ja: コーヒーのおかわり、いかがですか？
example.english: Would you like more coffee?

items.notes: Casual version: dou? Staff also say ikaga deshou ka, and ikaga deshita ka (how was it?).

items.english: shall I help?; want a hand?
items.use: Offers help to someone carrying, cooking or struggling with something.

example.romaji: omosou da ne. tetsudaou ka?
example.ja: 重そうだね。手伝おうか？
example.english: That looks heavy. Want a hand?

examplePolite.romaji: omosou desu ne. tetsudaimashou ka?
examplePolite.ja: 重そうですね。手伝いましょうか？
examplePolite.english: That looks heavy. Shall I help?

items.notes: Humbler still: otetsudai shimashou ka. Nanika tetsudau? means anything I can do?

items.use: Warmly lets someone go first, sit down or take something; doubling it makes it eager.

example.romaji: douzo douzo, saki ni haitte.
example.ja: どうぞどうぞ、先に入って。
example.english: Go ahead, you go in first.

examplePolite.romaji: douzo douzo, saki ni haitte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: どうぞどうぞ、先に入ってください。
examplePolite.english: Please, go on in first.

items.notes: A single douzo is the everyday here you go when handing something over.

items.english: let me know if you need anything
items.use: Friendly offer of ongoing help, said when leaving someone to get on with things.
items.ja: 何かあったら言ってね
items.kana: なにかあったらいってね
items.politeJa: 何かあったら言ってください

example.romaji: nanika attara itsu demo itte ne.
example.ja: 何かあったらいつでも言ってね。
example.english: If you need anything, just say so, anytime.

examplePolite.romaji: nanika attara itsu demo itte kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 何かあったらいつでも言ってくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please let me know anytime if you need anything.

items.notes: Literally if anything happens, tell me, so it's also said to someone sick or worried.

items.english: help yourself if you like; please have some
items.use: Offers food, a seat or a spare item without pressure, e.g. passing snacks round at work; answer arigatou, itadakimasu.

example.romaji: okashi katte kita kara, yokattara douzo.
example.ja: お菓子買ってきたから、よかったらどうぞ。
example.english: I bought some snacks, help yourselves.

examplePolite.romaji: omiyage desu. yokattara douzo.
examplePolite.ja: お土産です。よかったらどうぞ。
examplePolite.english: It's a little souvenir. Please have some.

blocks.label: Accepting kindness
blocks.rationale: Lets you accept an offer or gift gracefully.
blocks.interference: Ki o tsukawanaide sounds like a refusal but still ends in accepting.

items.english: are you sure?; is it really okay?
items.use: Checks that someone means it when they offer you something or do you a favour; follow with thanks.

example.romaji: e, ogori? ii no?
example.ja: え、おごり？いいの？
example.english: Wait, your treat? Are you sure?

examplePolite.romaji: e, ii n desu ka? arigatou gozaimasu.
examplePolite.ja: え、いいんですか？ありがとうございます。
examplePolite.english: Oh, are you sure? Thank you.

items.notes: Also asks permission after a -te verb: kore tabete ii no? (can I eat this?).

items.use: An eager yes to an invitation or a request for help.

example.romaji: sasotte kurete arigatou. yorokonde iku yo!
example.ja: 誘ってくれてありがとう。喜んで行くよ！
example.english: Thanks for inviting me. I'd love to come!

examplePolite.romaji: yorokonde otetsudai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 喜んでお手伝いします。
examplePolite.english: I'd be glad to help.

items.notes: Some izakaya staff shout hai, yorokonde! when they take an order.

items.english: don't go to any trouble; you didn't have to
items.use: Said when someone fusses over you or brings a gift; it's polite modesty, so still accept with thanks.
items.politeJa: 気を使わないでください

example.romaji: sonna ni ki o tsukawanaide yo.
example.ja: そんなに気を使わないでよ。
example.english: Oh, you didn't need to go to all that trouble.

examplePolite.romaji: douzo ki o tsukawanaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: どうぞ気を使わないでください。
examplePolite.english: Please don't go to any trouble.

items.notes: Formal set version: douzo okizukai naku. Ki o tsukau means to be considerate or fuss over someone.

blocks.label: Turning things down
blocks.rationale: Lets you say no politely without a long excuse.
blocks.interference: Kekkou desu is a firm no; enryo shite okimasu and kyou wa chotto are softer.

items.use: Firm, polite no to staff, salespeople or a host offering more; add iie or a reason to sound warmer.

example.romaji: iie, kekkou desu. mou juubun itadakimashita.
example.ja: いいえ、結構です。もう十分いただきました。
example.english: No, thank you. I've had plenty.

items.notes: Can sound cold to friends; use daijoubu instead. Kekkou also means quite: kekkou oishii (pretty tasty).

items.use: Turns down an invitation by trailing off; the unfinished sentence is the polite no, so no long excuse is needed.

example.romaji: gomen, kyou wa chotto... ashita nara ii yo.
example.ja: ごめん、今日はちょっと…明日ならいいよ。
example.english: Sorry, today's not great... tomorrow works, though.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, kyou wa chotto...
examplePolite.ja: すみません、今日はちょっと…
examplePolite.english: Sorry, today's a bit difficult...

items.notes: Chotto... alone works for any request you'd rather refuse.

items.use: Tells a taxi driver to stop, or tells someone walking or driving you that they needn't go further.

example.romaji: a, koko de ii desu. arigatou gozaimasu.
example.ja: あ、ここでいいです。ありがとうございます。
example.english: Oh, here's fine. Thank you.

items.notes: Clearer to a taxi driver: koko de tomete kudasai (please stop here).

items.use: Polite no to an offer or invitation, softer than kekkou desu.
items.kana: えんりょしておきます

example.romaji: kyou wa enryo shite okimasu. mata sasotte kudasai.
example.ja: 今日は遠慮しておきます。また誘ってください。
example.english: I'll pass today. Please ask me again.

items.notes: Casual version: enryo shitoku. Enryo means holding back.

blocks.label: Asking a favour
blocks.rationale: Lets you open a request and ask for help, casual or polite.
blocks.interference: Choudai and chotto tetsudatte are for close people; onegai dekimasu ka is the safe polite one.

items.use: Softens a favour or a no to a friend; say it first, then the request or refusal.

example.romaji: warui kedo, mado shimete kureru?
example.ja: 悪いけど、窓閉めてくれる？
example.english: Sorry, could you close the window?

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen ga, mado o shimete moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: すみませんが、窓を閉めてもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: Sorry, could you close the window?

items.notes: Warui ne afterwards means sorry about that.

items.use: Soft, homey request to family and close friends, after a thing (sore choudai) or a -te verb (matte choudai).

example.romaji: sore choudai! nodo kawaita.
example.ja: それちょうだい！喉渇いた。
example.english: Give me that! I'm thirsty.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, sore o kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、それをください。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, that one, please.

items.notes: Can sound childlike or motherly; adults asking strangers use kudasai.

items.english: give me a hand for a sec
items.use: Quick call for help to family, friends or a close coworker.
items.politeJa: ちょっと手伝ってもらえますか

example.romaji: chotto tetsudatte! kore omoi.
example.ja: ちょっと手伝って！これ重い。
example.english: Give me a hand! This is heavy.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, chotto tetsudatte moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: すみません、ちょっと手伝ってもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: Sorry, could you give me a hand?

items.notes: Add kureru? to soften it: chotto tetsudatte kureru?

items.romaji: onegai ga aru n da kedo
items.polite: onegai ga aru n desu ga
items.english: I have a favour to ask
items.use: Opens a bigger favour; the other person usually answers nani? and then you explain.
items.ja: お願いがあるんだけど
items.kana: おねがいがあるんだけど
items.politeJa: お願いがあるんですが

example.romaji: nee, chotto onegai ga aru n da kedo.
example.ja: ねえ、ちょっとお願いがあるんだけど。
example.english: Hey, I've got a favour to ask.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, onegai ga aru n desu ga.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、お願いがあるんですが。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, I have a favour to ask.

items.english: could you do that for me?; could I ask for...?
items.use: Polite request to staff, colleagues or strangers, after naming the thing or task.

example.romaji: kore, kopii onegai dekimasu ka?
example.ja: これ、コピーお願いできますか？
example.english: Could you make a copy of this for me?

items.notes: Casual version: onegai dekiru?

blocks.label: Leaving without buying
blocks.rationale: Lets you browse and walk away from a shop politely.
blocks.interference: Chotto kangaemasu usually means no, not a real maybe.

items.use: Answer to a shop assistant who asks if you're looking for something.

example.romaji: a, daijoubu desu. miteru dake desu.
example.ja: あ、大丈夫です。見てるだけです。
example.english: Oh, I'm fine. Just looking.

items.notes: Also means I'm only watching when someone asks you to join in.

items.use: Polite way to leave a shop or counter without buying now.

example.romaji: sumimasen, ato de mata kimasu.
example.ja: すみません、あとでまた来ます。
example.english: Sorry, I'll come back later.

items.notes: Casual version: mata kuru ne.

items.use: Polite way to leave without buying or to end a sales pitch; it usually means no.
items.kana: ちょっとかんがえます

example.romaji: sou desu ne... chotto kangaemasu.
example.ja: そうですね…ちょっと考えます。
example.english: Hmm... I'll think about it.

items.notes: Casual version: chotto kangaete miru.

blocks.label: Drinking together
blocks.rationale: Lets you toast, order rounds and groan about it later.
blocks.interference: Mou ippai is one more drink; ippai alone also means full.

items.use: The toast that starts the drinking; wait until everyone has a glass before the first sip.

example.romaji: jaa minna, otsukaresama! kanpai!
example.ja: じゃあみんな、お疲れさま！乾杯！
example.english: Okay everyone, good work today! Cheers!

examplePolite.romaji: dewa minasan, kanpai shimashou.
examplePolite.ja: では皆さん、乾杯しましょう。
examplePolite.english: Well, everyone, let's raise a toast.

items.notes: At work dinners someone usually gives a short toast speech first.

items.use: Orders or offers another glass or bowl; add kudasai to staff.

example.romaji: mou ippai nomou yo.
example.ja: もう一杯飲もうよ。
example.english: Let's have one more.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, biiru mou ippai kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、ビールもう一杯ください。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, another beer, please.

items.notes: Ippai on its own also means full or lots; the mou tells you it's one more.

items.use: Groaned the night of or the morning after.

example.romaji: kinou nomisugita... atama itai.
example.ja: 昨日飲み過ぎた…頭痛い。
example.english: I drank too much last night... my head hurts.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou wa chotto nomisugimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日はちょっと飲み過ぎました。
examplePolite.english: I had a bit too much to drink yesterday.

items.notes: -sugita works on any verb: tabesugita (ate too much). A hangover is futsukayoi.

items.use: The classic first order at an izakaya so the group can toast quickly; food comes after.
items.politeJa: とりあえずビールお願いします

example.romaji: minna, toriaezu biiru de ii?
example.ja: みんな、とりあえずビールでいい？
example.english: Beer to start for everyone?

examplePolite.romaji: toriaezu biiru mittsu onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: とりあえずビール三つお願いします。
examplePolite.english: Three beers to start, please.

items.notes: Toriaezu alone means for now: toriaezu ikou (let's just go for now).

blocks.label: Paying the bill
blocks.rationale: Lets you treat someone, ask for the bill, a receipt or separate payment.
blocks.interference: Ryoushuusho is the formal expense receipt, not the till slip (reshiito).

items.use: Offers to pay for a friend's food or drinks; they usually answer ii no? before accepting.

example.romaji: kyou wa watashi ga ogoru yo.
example.ja: 今日は私がおごるよ。
example.english: Today's on me.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa watashi ga gochisou shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は私がごちそうします。
examplePolite.english: Today's my treat.

items.notes: The treat itself is ogori; ogotte means treat me.

items.use: Asks restaurant or bar staff for the bill; at many places you then pay at the register (reji) by the exit.
items.kana: おかいけいおねがいします

example.romaji: sumimasen, okaikei onegai shimasu.
example.ja: すみません、お会計お願いします。
example.english: Excuse me, could we get the bill?

items.notes: Okanjou onegai shimasu is also common at izakaya.

items.use: Asks for a formal receipt for expenses at shops, restaurants and taxis; staff may then ask what name to write.
items.kana: りょうしゅうしょおねがいします

example.romaji: sumimasen, ryoushuusho onegai shimasu.
example.ja: すみません、領収書お願いします。
example.english: Excuse me, could I get a receipt?

items.notes: A reshiito is the printed till slip; a ryoushuusho is the formal one for claiming expenses.

items.use: Asks to pay separately at the register; staff may ask goissho de yoroshii desu ka? (together?).
items.kana: べつべつでおねがいします

example.romaji: okaikei wa betsubetsu de onegai shimasu.
example.ja: お会計は別々でお願いします。
example.english: We'll pay separately, please.

items.notes: Splitting the total evenly among friends is warikan.

blocks.label: Inviting someone to eat
blocks.rationale: Lets you suggest a drink, a meal or a coffee and plan what to eat.
blocks.interference: Gohan ikanai? is eating out; nani taberu? is choosing the food.

items.english: want to go for a drink?
items.use: Invites a friend or coworker out drinking; the negative question makes it easy to say no.

example.romaji: shigoto owattara, nomi ni ikanai?
example.ja: 仕事終わったら、飲みに行かない？
example.english: Want to go for a drink after work?

examplePolite.romaji: kondo, nomi ni ikimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今度、飲みに行きませんか？
examplePolite.english: Would you like to go for a drink sometime?

items.notes: A nomikai is an organised drinking party with work or a club.

items.english: how about a tea or something?; want to grab a coffee?
items.use: Low-pressure invitation to sit and chat over a drink, at home or at a cafe.
items.politeJa: お茶でもいかがですか

example.romaji: jikan aru nara, ocha demo dou?
example.ja: 時間あるなら、お茶でもどう？
example.english: If you've got time, how about a coffee?

examplePolite.romaji: yokattara, ocha demo ikaga desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: よかったら、お茶でもいかがですか？
examplePolite.english: If you like, would you care for some tea?

items.notes: Ocha suru means stopping at a cafe, not only drinking tea.

items.english: what shall we eat?; what are you having?
items.use: Asks a friend what they want for a meal or what they're ordering.

example.romaji: hirugohan, nani taberu? ramen?
example.ja: 昼ご飯、何食べる？ラーメン？
example.english: What should we have for lunch? Ramen?

examplePolite.romaji: kyou no hirugohan, nani tabemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今日の昼ご飯、何食べますか？
examplePolite.english: What are you having for lunch today?

items.notes: With a menu in hand, nani ni suru? (what are you getting?) is just as common.

items.english: anything you don't eat?; are you picky?
items.use: A host or friend asks before cooking or ordering; answer tokuni nai (nothing really) or name the food.
items.politeJa: 好き嫌いはありますか

example.romaji: kyou wa uchi de tsukuru kedo, suki kirai aru?
example.ja: 今日はうちで作るけど、好き嫌いある？
example.english: I'm cooking tonight. Anything you don't eat?

examplePolite.romaji: nanika suki kirai wa arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 何か好き嫌いはありますか？
examplePolite.english: Is there anything you don't eat?

items.notes: For allergies say arerugii ga arimasu.

items.use: Casual invitation to eat out with a friend or coworker; the ni is dropped.

example.romaji: kondo no doyoubi, gohan ikanai?
example.ja: 今度の土曜日、ご飯行かない？
example.english: Want to get something to eat this Saturday?

examplePolite.romaji: yokattara, kondo gohan ikimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: よかったら、今度ご飯行きませんか？
examplePolite.english: If you're free, would you like to get a meal sometime?

items.notes: Kondo gohan ikou ne can be a vague pleasantry rather than a real plan.

blocks.label: Handing over money
blocks.rationale: Lets you follow the cashier as you pay and get your change.
blocks.interference: Oazukari shimasu names the money you handed over, not the total you owe.

items.use: The cashier says the amount first, then okaeshi desu, as they hand you the change.

example.romaji: sanbyaku nijuu en no okaeshi desu.
example.ja: 320円のお返しです。
example.english: Here's 320 yen in change.

items.notes: Okaeshi also means a return gift for a present you received.

items.english: out of (the amount you hand over); I'll take that for you
items.use: The cashier says it with the money you handed over: sen en oazukari shimasu means out of 1,000 yen.

example.romaji: ichiman en oazukari shimasu.
example.ja: 一万円お預かりします。
example.english: Out of 10,000 yen.

items.notes: Also said when staff take your coat, bag or card to hold for you.

items.english: all on one bill?; all together?
items.use: Asked at the register when a group pays; answer hai, or betsubetsu de (separately).
items.ja: ご一緒でよろしいですか
items.kana: ごいっしょでよろしいですか

example.romaji: okaikei wa goissho de yoroshii desu ka?
example.ja: お会計はご一緒でよろしいですか？
example.english: Will that be on one bill?

items.notes: In shops it can also mean all in one bag?

items.use: Asked when you pay by credit card, since installments are an option; answer hai.
items.ja: 一括でよろしいですか
items.kana: いっかつでよろしいですか

example.romaji: kaado de desu ne. ikkatsu de yoroshii desu ka?
example.ja: カードでですね。一括でよろしいですか？
example.english: By card, then. In one payment?

items.notes: Bunkatsu means installments; you almost always want ikkatsu.

blocks.label: Shop greetings
blocks.rationale: Lets you understand staff as you browse, ask for help and leave.
blocks.interference: Nanika osagashi desu ka (looking for something?) versus nanika goyou desu ka (what do you need?).

items.use: Staff say it as you leave a shop or restaurant; no reply needed, or gochisousama deshita after a meal.

example.romaji: arigatou gozaimashita. mata okoshi kudasai.
example.ja: ありがとうございました。またお越しください。
example.english: Thank you very much. Please come again.

items.notes: Often heard as mata okoshi kudasaimase, even more polite.

items.english: are you looking for something?; can I help you find anything?
items.use: Shop staff ask it while you browse; answer miteru dake desu (just looking) or name what you want.
items.kana: なにかおさがしですか

example.romaji: irasshaimase. nanika osagashi desu ka?
example.ja: いらっしゃいませ。何かお探しですか？
example.english: Hello. Are you looking for anything?

items.use: Shop staff, guides and presenters say it to point you at something; also common in announcements.

example.romaji: kochira no shashin o goran kudasai.
example.ja: こちらの写真をご覧ください。
example.english: Please take a look at this photo.

items.notes: The respectful form of mite kudasai. Douzo goran kudasai means feel free to look around.

items.english: can I help you?; what do you need?
items.use: Staff or a receptionist ask it when you walk up, or someone asks it at the door; say what you want.

example.romaji: sumimasen, nanika goyou desu ka?
example.ja: すみません、何かご用ですか？
example.english: Excuse me, can I help you?

items.notes: Goyou means your business or errand. From a stranger it can sound cool, like what do you want here?

items.english: thanks as always; hi there (shopkeeper's greeting)
items.use: Shopkeepers say maido arigatou gozaimasu to customers; in Osaka a bare maido! is a friendly hello.
items.politeJa: 毎度ありがとうございます

example.romaji: maido! kyou wa nani ni suru?
example.ja: 毎度！今日は何にする？
example.english: Hi there! What'll it be today?

examplePolite.romaji: maido arigatou gozaimasu. mata okoshi kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 毎度ありがとうございます。またお越しください。
examplePolite.english: Thank you as always. Please come again.

items.notes: Literally every time. Maido ari is the clipped market-stall version.

blocks.label: Making plans
blocks.rationale: Lets you settle a day, time and place with a friend, and back out if you must.
blocks.interference: Itsu (when, which day) versus nanji (what time).

items.use: Asked when making plans; answer with a place, or suggest one: eki de ii?
items.politeJa: どこで会いましょうか

example.romaji: doyoubi, doko de au? shibuya de ii?
example.ja: 土曜日、どこで会う？渋谷でいい？
example.english: Where shall we meet on Saturday? Is Shibuya okay?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa doko de aimashou ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日はどこで会いましょうか？
examplePolite.english: Where shall we meet tomorrow?

items.notes: Machiawase is the arrangement to meet; machiawase basho is the meeting spot.

items.english: when works for you?; when's good?
items.use: Asked when setting a date; answer with a day + ga ii, or X wa dou?

example.romaji: kondo nomi ni ikou yo. itsu ga ii?
example.ja: 今度飲みに行こうよ。いつがいい？
example.english: Let's go for a drink sometime. When works for you?

examplePolite.romaji: uchiawase wa itsu ga ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 打ち合わせはいつがいいですか？
examplePolite.english: When is good for the meeting?

items.notes: At work, itsu ga yoroshii desu ka is more polite.

items.use: Asked once you've picked a day; answer with a time, or suggest one: rokuji wa dou?

example.romaji: doyoubi ne. jaa, nanji ga ii?
example.ja: 土曜日ね。じゃあ、何時がいい？
example.english: Saturday, then. So what time works for you?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa nanji ga ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日は何時がいいですか？
examplePolite.english: What time is good for you tomorrow?

items.notes: Nanji is what time; don't confuse it with nanjikan (how many hours).

items.english: go on ahead; go without me
items.use: Said when you'll catch up later; the other person may answer jaa, matteru ne.
items.politeJa: 先に行っていてください

example.romaji: wasuremono shita. saki ni ittete!
example.ja: 忘れ物した。先に行ってて！
example.english: I forgot something. Go on ahead!

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, saki ni itte ite kudasai. sugu oikakemasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、先に行っていてください。すぐ追いかけます。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, please go on ahead. I'll catch up soon.

items.notes: Don't mix it up with osaki ni, which you say when you leave before others.

items.english: I can't make it after all
items.use: Said to cancel a plan you agreed to, usually with gomen and a short reason.

example.romaji: gomen, kyuu ni shigoto ga haitte ikenaku natta.
example.ja: ごめん、急に仕事が入って行けなくなった。
example.english: Sorry, something came up at work and I can't make it.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, ashita ikenaku narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、明日行けなくなりました。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I can't make it tomorrow after all.

items.notes: The -naku natta ending says things changed, which sounds softer than a flat ikenai.

blocks.label: Keeping in touch
blocks.rationale: Lets you start, keep up and wind down contact with friends.
blocks.interference: Mata renraku suru ne can be a polite brush-off rather than a promise.

items.english: I'll be in touch; I'll get back to you
items.use: Said when ending a chat or call without a fixed plan; it can also be a soft no to an invitation.

example.romaji: jaa, yotei ga wakattara mata renraku suru ne.
example.ja: じゃあ、予定がわかったらまた連絡するね。
example.english: Okay, I'll get back to you once I know my plans.

examplePolite.romaji: kakunin shite, mata renraku shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 確認して、また連絡します。
examplePolite.english: I'll check and get back to you.

items.notes: Renraku means contact; renraku shite means get in touch with me.

items.english: what are you up to?; what are you doing now?
items.use: An opening text or call to a friend or partner, often before inviting them out.

example.romaji: ima nani shiteru? hima nara gohan ikanai?
example.ja: 今何してる？暇ならご飯行かない？
example.english: What are you up to? If you're free, want to grab food?

items.notes: A common answer is betsu ni or nani mo shitenai (nothing much).

items.use: LINE is Japan's main messaging app; said at a goodbye or when you want an update.

example.romaji: tsuitara rain shite ne.
example.ja: 着いたらLINEしてね。
example.english: Message me when you get there.

examplePolite.romaji: nanika attara rain kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 何かあったらLINEください。
examplePolite.english: Message me if anything comes up.

items.notes: LINE works as a suru verb: rain suru, rain shita. Meeru shite is the older email version.

items.use: Said to someone new you want to keep in touch with; you then scan each other's QR code.
items.kana: ラインこうかんしよう

example.romaji: kyou tanoshikatta! rain koukan shiyou yo.
example.ja: 今日楽しかった！LINE交換しようよ。
example.english: Today was fun! Let's swap LINE.

examplePolite.romaji: yokattara, rain koukan shimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: よかったら、LINE交換しませんか？
examplePolite.english: If you like, shall we exchange LINE contacts?

items.notes: Renrakusaki koukan is the general version: swapping contact details.

blocks.label: Starting a call
blocks.rationale: Lets you open a call and cope with a bad line, a low battery or an unknown caller.
blocks.interference: Kikoeru (can hear) versus kiku (listen, ask).

items.english: is now a good time?; got a minute?
items.use: Asked at the start of a call or before interrupting someone; answer un, daijoubu or gomen, ato de.

example.romaji: moshimoshi, ima daijoubu? chotto kikitai koto ga atte.
example.ja: もしもし、今大丈夫？ちょっと聞きたいことがあって。
example.english: Hi, is now a good time? There's something I want to ask.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, ima daijoubu desu ka? sugu sumimasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、今大丈夫ですか？すぐ済みます。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, do you have a moment? It won't take long.

items.notes: To a boss or client, ima ojikan yoroshii desu ka is safer.

items.use: Said on a bad phone or video call; the answer is kikoeru yo or kikoenai.

example.romaji: moshimoshi? kikoeru? denpa warui mitai.
example.ja: もしもし？聞こえる？電波悪いみたい。
example.english: Hello? Can you hear me? The signal seems bad.

examplePolite.romaji: moshimoshi, kikoemasu ka? koe ga tooi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: もしもし、聞こえますか？声が遠いですね。
examplePolite.english: Hello, can you hear me? You sound far away.

items.notes: Kikoeru means can be heard, so the sound takes ga: koe ga kikoeru. It also asks did you hear that? about a noise.

items.english: who is this?; may I ask who's calling?
items.use: Asked politely on the phone or at the door when the person is unknown; answer with your name + desu.

example.romaji: shitsurei desu ga, dochirasama desu ka?
example.ja: 失礼ですが、どちら様ですか？
example.english: Excuse me, but may I ask who's calling?

items.notes: The casual dare? sounds blunt to a stranger. Business calls often use dochirasama deshou ka.

items.use: Said to warn that a call or chat may cut off soon.

example.romaji: yabai, juuden kiresou. ato de kakenaosu ne.
example.ja: やばい、充電切れそう。後でかけ直すね。
example.english: Ugh, my battery's about to die. I'll call you back.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, juuden ga kiresou desu. ato de renraku shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、充電が切れそうです。後で連絡します。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, my battery's almost dead. I'll get in touch later.

items.notes: Juuden kireta means it died; a charger is juudenki.

blocks.label: Get well soon
blocks.rationale: Lets you say the right thing to someone sick, tired or leaving for a while.
blocks.interference: Odaiji ni is only for illness; karada ni ki o tsukete is the general take care.

items.use: Said to someone sick or hurt as you part; clinic and pharmacy staff say it as you leave, and you answer arigatou gozaimasu.

example.romaji: kaze hiita no? odaiji ni ne.
example.ja: 風邪ひいたの？お大事にね。
example.english: You caught a cold? Get well soon.

examplePolite.romaji: kaze desu ka? douzo odaiji ni.
examplePolite.ja: 風邪ですか？どうぞお大事に。
examplePolite.english: A cold? Please take care.

items.notes: Only for illness or injury, not a general goodbye.

items.english: don't overdo it; don't push yourself
items.use: Said to someone sick, tired or overworking; also to let someone off an invitation.
items.politeJa: 無理しないでください

example.romaji: netsu aru n desho? muri shinaide ne.
example.ja: 熱あるんでしょ？無理しないでね。
example.english: You've got a fever, right? Don't push yourself.

examplePolite.romaji: isogashii to omoimasu ga, muri shinaide kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 忙しいと思いますが、無理しないでくださいね。
examplePolite.english: I know you're busy, but please don't overdo it.

items.notes: Muri means too much or impossible; muri! on its own means no way!

items.use: Said to someone sick, tired, or done with a hard stretch of work.
items.politeJa: ゆっくり休んでください

example.romaji: kyou wa hayaku nete, yukkuri yasunde ne.
example.ja: 今日は早く寝て、ゆっくり休んでね。
example.english: Go to bed early tonight and get some good rest.

examplePolite.romaji: konshuu wa taihen deshita ne. yukkuri yasunde kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 今週は大変でしたね。ゆっくり休んでください。
examplePolite.english: This week was tough. Please get some good rest.

items.notes: Yasumu means rest, and also take a day off.

items.polite: okarada ni ki o tsukete kudasai
items.english: look after yourself; take care of your health
items.use: Said at a goodbye before a long gap, or to someone busy or getting older; also ends letters.
items.politeJa: お体に気をつけてください

example.romaji: samuku natta kara, karada ni ki o tsukete ne.
example.ja: 寒くなったから、体に気をつけてね。
example.english: It's gotten cold, so look after yourself.

examplePolite.romaji: isogashii jiki desu ga, okarada ni ki o tsukete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 忙しい時期ですが、お体に気をつけてください。
examplePolite.english: It's a busy time, but please take care of yourself.

items.notes: Ki o tsukete alone means be careful, or take care as a goodbye.

blocks.label: Cheering someone up
blocks.rationale: Lets you comfort someone who's down and praise their effort.
blocks.interference: Faito means keep going, not fight; ganbatte is the everyday cheer.

items.use: Said to show you understand someone's frustration or sadness, often with yo.

example.romaji: sore wa kuyashii yo ne. kimochi wakaru.
example.ja: それは悔しいよね。気持ちわかる。
example.english: That's so frustrating. I know how you feel.

examplePolite.romaji: sono kimochi, yoku wakarimasu.
examplePolite.ja: その気持ち、よくわかります。
examplePolite.english: I really understand how you feel.

items.notes: Wakaru wakaru is a quick, casual I get it.

items.english: you did really well; great effort
items.use: Praise after someone finishes something hard, win or lose; often to kids or juniors.

example.romaji: shiai, oshikatta kedo yoku ganbatta ne.
example.ja: 試合、惜しかったけどよく頑張ったね。
example.english: The game was close, but you did really well.

examplePolite.romaji: nagai aida, yoku ganbarimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: 長い間、よく頑張りましたね。
examplePolite.english: You worked so hard for so long.

items.notes: It praises effort, not results. To a superior, otsukaresama deshita is safer.

items.use: Said to someone sad or discouraged, often after a failure or a breakup.
items.politeJa: 元気を出してください

example.romaji: sonna ni ochikomanaide. genki dashite yo.
example.ja: そんなに落ち込まないで。元気出してよ。
example.english: Don't be so down. Cheer up.

examplePolite.romaji: tsugi ga arimasu yo. genki o dashite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 次がありますよ。元気を出してください。
examplePolite.english: There's always next time. Please cheer up.

items.notes: Genki here means energy or spirits; genki nai ne means you seem down.

items.english: go for it!; you can do it!
items.use: Called out to cheer someone on in sport or before a challenge.

example.romaji: ashita shiken desho? faito!
example.ja: 明日試験でしょ？ファイト！
example.english: Your exam's tomorrow, right? You've got this!

items.notes: From English fight, but it means keep going. Ganbatte is the everyday word.

blocks.label: Calming someone down
blocks.rationale: Lets you soothe someone who is panicking or crying, and react to sad news.
blocks.interference: Kawaisou (poor thing) versus kawaii (cute).

items.use: Said to someone panicking, angry or rushing; soothing when said softly, sharp when shouted.

example.romaji: chotto ochitsuite. yukkuri hanashite.
example.ja: ちょっと落ち着いて。ゆっくり話して。
example.english: Calm down a bit. Talk slowly.

examplePolite.romaji: daijoubu desu kara, ochitsuite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 大丈夫ですから、落ち着いてください。
examplePolite.english: It's okay, so please calm down.

items.notes: Ochitsuita describes a calm person or a quiet, relaxed place.

items.use: Said about a person or animal in a sad situation; to someone's face it can sound pitying.

example.romaji: sono neko, kega shiteru. kawaisou ni.
example.ja: その猫、ケガしてる。かわいそうに。
example.english: That cat's hurt. Poor thing.

items.notes: Kawaisou means pitiful; don't mix it up with kawaii (cute).

items.english: there, there; good boy, good girl
items.use: Said while patting a crying child or a pet; to an adult only as a joke.

example.romaji: yoshi yoshi, mou daijoubu da yo.
example.ja: よしよし、もう大丈夫だよ。
example.english: There, there, it's all right now.

items.notes: A single yoshi! means right!, said when starting something.

items.use: Said gently to someone crying, often a child or partner.

example.romaji: mou nakanaide. watashi ga iru kara.
example.ja: もう泣かないで。私がいるから。
example.english: Don't cry anymore. I'm here for you.

examplePolite.romaji: douka nakanaide kudasai. daijoubu desu kara.
examplePolite.ja: どうか泣かないでください。大丈夫ですから。
examplePolite.english: Please don't cry. It's going to be okay.

items.notes: The -naide ending means don't, as in shinpai shinaide and muri shinaide.

blocks.label: That sounds hard
blocks.rationale: Show sympathy when someone has had a rough time.
blocks.interference: taihen is hassle and effort; tsurai is emotional pain.

items.english: that must have been hard; what an ordeal
items.use: Sympathy after someone tells you about a rough time; often followed by daijoubu?

example.romaji: sore wa taihen datta ne. mou daijoubu?
example.ja: それは大変だったね。もう大丈夫？
example.english: That must have been rough. Are you okay now?

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa taihen deshita ne. mou daijoubu desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: それは大変でしたね。もう大丈夫ですか？
examplePolite.english: That must have been hard. Are you all right now?

items.notes: For something still going on, say taihen da ne (that's tough).

items.english: that sounds really hard; that must hurt
items.use: Sympathy for emotional pain: a breakup, a loss, a painful situation.

example.romaji: wakareta no? sore wa tsurai ne.
example.ja: 別れたの？それはつらいね。
example.english: You broke up? That must really hurt.

examplePolite.romaji: wakareta n desu ka. sore wa tsurai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 別れたんですか。それはつらいですね。
examplePolite.english: You broke up? That must be hard.

items.notes: taihen is about hassle and effort; tsurai is about pain.

items.english: don't let it get you down; don't lose heart
items.use: Comfort after a failure or disappointment, like a lost game or a rejection.
items.politeJa: 気を落とさないでください

example.romaji: tsugi ga aru kara, ki o otosanaide.
example.ja: 次があるから、気を落とさないで。
example.english: There's always next time, don't let it get you down.

examplePolite.romaji: tsugi ga arimasu kara, ki o otosanaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 次がありますから、気を落とさないでください。
examplePolite.english: There will be a next time, so please don't lose heart.

items.notes: Friends often say ki ni shinaide (don't worry about it) instead.

blocks.label: Take it easy, get well
blocks.rationale: Show care for someone who is rushed or unwell.
blocks.interference: None.

items.use: Reassures someone who is hurrying or panicking.
items.politeJa: 焦らなくていいですよ

example.romaji: jikan aru kara, aseranakute ii yo.
example.ja: 時間あるから、焦らなくていいよ。
example.english: We've got time, no need to rush.

examplePolite.romaji: jikan wa arimasu kara, aseranakute ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 時間はありますから、焦らなくていいですよ。
examplePolite.english: There's time, so no need to rush.

items.notes: Built from aseru (to panic, rush) plus -nakute ii (you don't have to).

items.use: To someone sick or injured, as you leave or end a call.
items.politeJa: 早く良くなってくださいね

example.romaji: kaze? hayaku yoku natte ne.
example.ja: 風邪？早く良くなってね。
example.english: A cold? Get better soon.

examplePolite.romaji: hayaku yoku natte kudasai ne. odaiji ni.
examplePolite.ja: 早く良くなってくださいね。お大事に。
examplePolite.english: Get well soon. Take care.

items.notes: odaiji ni (take care of yourself) is the standard set phrase to anyone unwell.

items.polite: kaze o hikanai you ni ki o tsukete kudasai
items.english: don't catch a cold; stay warm
items.use: A caring send-off when it's cold or someone's heading out in the rain.
items.ja: 風邪ひかないようにね
items.kana: かぜひかないようにね
items.politeJa: 風邪をひかないように気をつけてください

example.romaji: kyou samui kara, kaze hikanai you ni ne.
example.ja: 今日寒いから、風邪ひかないようにね。
example.english: It's cold today, so don't catch a cold.

examplePolite.romaji: kaze o hikanai you ni ki o tsukete kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 風邪をひかないように気をつけてくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Be careful not to catch a cold.

items.notes: Catching a cold is kaze o hiku, literally 'pull a cold'.

blocks.label: Congratulations
blocks.rationale: Congratulate birthdays, weddings, exams and graduations.
blocks.interference: Polite forms add go- to kekkon and sotsugyou, but not to goukaku.

items.use: The answer is arigatou; add gozaimasu for anyone you speak politely to.
items.kana: おたんじょうびおめでとう
items.politeJa: お誕生日おめでとうございます

example.romaji: otanjoubi omedetou! kyou wa ogoru yo.
example.ja: お誕生日おめでとう！今日はおごるよ。
example.english: Happy birthday! Today's on me.

examplePolite.romaji: otanjoubi omedetou gozaimasu. kyou wa watashi ga gochisou shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: お誕生日おめでとうございます。今日は私がごちそうします。
examplePolite.english: Happy birthday. Today is my treat.

items.notes: Friends often shorten it to tanjoubi omedetou or just omedetou.

items.use: To a friend getting married; the polite form with go- is what goes on cards and at the reception.
items.politeJa: ご結婚おめでとうございます

example.romaji: kekkon omedetou! shiawase ni ne.
example.ja: 結婚おめでとう！幸せにね。
example.english: Congrats on getting married! Be happy.

examplePolite.romaji: gokekkon omedetou gozaimasu. oshiawase ni.
examplePolite.ja: ご結婚おめでとうございます。お幸せに。
examplePolite.english: Congratulations on your marriage. Wishing you every happiness.

items.use: For passing an entrance exam, a certification test, or an audition.
items.politeJa: 合格おめでとうございます

example.romaji: goukaku omedetou! yoku ganbatta ne.
example.ja: 合格おめでとう！よく頑張ったね。
example.english: Congrats on passing! You worked so hard.

examplePolite.romaji: goukaku omedetou gozaimasu. yoku ganbarimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: 合格おめでとうございます。よく頑張りましたね。
examplePolite.english: Congratulations on passing. You worked really hard.

items.use: Heard most in March, Japan's graduation season.
items.kana: そつぎょうおめでとう
items.politeJa: ご卒業おめでとうございます

example.romaji: sotsugyou omedetou! haru kara shakaijin da ne.
example.ja: 卒業おめでとう！春から社会人だね。
example.english: Congrats on graduating! You start working this spring.

examplePolite.romaji: gosotsugyou omedetou gozaimasu. haru kara oshigoto desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: ご卒業おめでとうございます。春からお仕事ですね。
examplePolite.english: Congratulations on graduating. You start work in spring, right?

blocks.label: Oh and whoa sounds
blocks.rationale: Make the quick noises that show surprise.
blocks.interference: ara is mild surprise; arara is 'oh dear' at a mishap.

items.use: Shock or amazement; with a grimace it means disgust.

example.romaji: uwa, kyou hito ga ooi na!
example.ja: うわっ、今日人が多いな！
example.english: Whoa, it's so crowded today!

examplePolite.romaji: uwa, kyou wa hito ga ooi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: うわっ、今日は人が多いですね。
examplePolite.english: Wow, it's really crowded today.

items.notes: Drawn out, uwaa is awe: uwaa, kirei (wow, beautiful).

items.use: A light 'oh' when you notice something good or see someone arrive.

example.romaji: o! ii no aru jan.
example.ja: おっ！いいのあるじゃん。
example.english: Oh! There's a good one.

examplePolite.romaji: o, ii no ga arimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: おっ、いいのがありますね。
examplePolite.english: Oh, there's a nice one.

items.notes: a! is for sudden realization or alarm; o! is for pleasant noticing.

items.use: Mild surprise, typically from women, like running into someone you know.

example.romaji: ara, hisashiburi ne. genki?
example.ja: あら、久しぶりね。元気？
example.english: Oh, long time no see. How are you?

examplePolite.romaji: ara, ohisashiburi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あら、お久しぶりですね。
examplePolite.english: Oh, it's been a long time.

items.notes: Men rarely say it; are? is the neutral 'huh?'.

items.use: Sympathetic or teasing reaction to a small mishap, usually someone else's.

example.romaji: arara, juusu koboshichatta ne.
example.ja: あらら、ジュースこぼしちゃったね。
example.english: Oh dear, you spilled your juice.

examplePolite.romaji: arara, juusu ga koborete shimaimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: あらら、ジュースがこぼれてしまいましたね。
examplePolite.english: Oh dear, the juice spilled.

blocks.label: Hmm and huh sounds
blocks.rationale: Show you're listening, or that you're not impressed.
blocks.interference: Drawn out, fuun, hai hai and haa can all sound rude.

items.use: A listener's 'I see', but it can sound unimpressed or doubtful.

example.romaji: fuun, sou nan da.
example.ja: ふーん、そうなんだ。
example.english: Hmm, is that right.

items.notes: To elders say naruhodo or sou nan desu ne; fuun can sound rude.

items.use: A quick double yes; drawn out, it brushes someone off.

example.romaji: hai hai, wakatta yo.
example.ja: はいはい、わかったよ。
example.english: Yeah, yeah, I get it.

items.notes: Said quick and bright it's a friendly 'yes, yes', even on the phone; never drawn out to a superior.

items.use: Opens a comment with feeling; also a bashful start to answering praise.

example.romaji: iyaa, kyou wa atsui ne.
example.ja: いやー、今日は暑いね。
example.english: Man, it's hot today.

examplePolite.romaji: iyaa, kyou wa atsui desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: いやー、今日は暑いですね。
examplePolite.english: My, it's hot today.

items.notes: Not 'no': short iya means no, drawn-out iyaa is a filler.

items.use: Rising and sharp, it's an annoyed 'huh?!'; long and falling, it's a sigh.

example.romaji: haa? nani itten no?
example.ja: はあ？何言ってんの？
example.english: Huh? What are you talking about?

items.notes: A flat haa to a request is a reluctant 'uh, okay'; the rising haa? is rude.

blocks.label: Praising someone
blocks.rationale: Cheer someone else's success or good luck.
blocks.interference: yoku yatta talks down, so not to a boss.

items.english: you did it!; way to go
items.use: Congratulates a friend on a success; yatta alone is your own win.

example.romaji: goukaku shita no? yatta ne!
example.ja: 合格したの？やったね！
example.english: You passed? You did it!

examplePolite.romaji: goukaku shita n desu ka? yarimashita ne!
examplePolite.ja: 合格したんですか？やりましたね！
examplePolite.english: You passed? That's great!

items.use: Praise from a parent, coach, or boss to someone below them.

example.romaji: yoku yatta! zenbu hitori de yatta no?
example.ja: よくやった！全部一人でやったの？
example.english: Well done! You did it all by yourself?

examplePolite.romaji: yoku yarimashita ne. taihen datta deshou.
examplePolite.ja: よくやりましたね。大変だったでしょう。
examplePolite.english: Well done. That must have been tough.

items.notes: It talks down, so don't say it to a boss; use otsukaresama deshita instead.

items.english: lucky you; I'm jealous; that's nice
items.use: Wistful reaction to someone's good news or to something you wish you had.

example.romaji: ii naa, hawai iku no?
example.ja: いいなあ、ハワイ行くの？
example.english: Lucky you, you're going to Hawaii?

examplePolite.romaji: ii desu ne, hawai ni iku n desu ka.
examplePolite.ja: いいですね、ハワイに行くんですか。
examplePolite.english: How nice, you're going to Hawaii?

items.notes: The polite ii desu ne loses the hint of envy.

items.use: Quick praise for a good move, shot, or idea, often in sports and games.

example.romaji: naisu! ima no shuuto, sugoi yo.
example.ja: ナイス！今のシュート、すごいよ。
example.english: Nice! That shot was amazing.

examplePolite.romaji: naisu desu! ima no shuuto, sugokatta desu.
examplePolite.ja: ナイスです！今のシュート、すごかったです。
examplePolite.english: Nice! That shot was great.

items.notes: Often joined to a noun: naisu aidia (nice idea), naisu shotto.

blocks.label: Looks good
blocks.rationale: Approve of how something looks or is going.
blocks.interference: It's yosasou, not ii sou.

items.use: Approves of how something looks, feels, or is coming along.

example.romaji: un, ii kanji! sono mama tsuzukete.
example.ja: うん、いい感じ！そのまま続けて。
example.english: Yeah, looks good! Keep going like that.

examplePolite.romaji: ii kanji desu ne. sono mama tsuzukete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: いい感じですね。そのまま続けてください。
examplePolite.english: That's looking good. Please keep going.

items.notes: About a person it means likable: ii kanji no hito (a nice person).

items.use: Approves of something; with a shrug it pushes 'why not, go for it'.

example.romaji: ii jan, sono fuku. niau yo.
example.ja: いいじゃん、その服。似合うよ。
example.english: Nice outfit. It suits you.

examplePolite.romaji: ii ja nai desu ka, sono fuku. niaimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: いいじゃないですか、その服。似合いますよ。
examplePolite.english: That outfit's nice. It suits you.

items.notes: The 'why not' use: ii jan, ikou yo (come on, let's go).

items.use: Judges by looks or description, before you've tried it.

example.romaji: kono mise, yosasou da ne.
example.ja: この店、よさそうだね。
example.english: This place looks good.

examplePolite.romaji: kono mise, yosasou desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この店、よさそうですね。
examplePolite.english: This place looks nice.

items.notes: Not ii sou: the 'looks' form of ii is irregular.

items.use: Excited when you find exactly what you wanted.

example.romaji: kore kore! kono aji ga tabetakatta.
example.ja: これこれ！この味が食べたかった。
example.english: This is it! This is the taste I've been craving.

examplePolite.romaji: kore kore! kono aji ga tabetakatta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: これこれ！この味が食べたかったんです。
examplePolite.english: This is it! This is the taste I wanted.

items.notes: From an older person to a child, it's a gentle 'now, now' scolding.

blocks.label: Forget it, whatever
blocks.rationale: Drop a topic or brush something off.
blocks.interference: dou demo ii (I don't care) vs nan demo ii (anything is fine).

items.use: Ends an argument or a request in frustration; it can sound cold.

example.romaji: mou ii, jibun de yaru.
example.ja: もういい、自分でやる。
example.english: Forget it, I'll do it myself.

examplePolite.romaji: mou ii desu. jibun de yarimasu.
examplePolite.ja: もういいです。自分でやります。
examplePolite.english: Never mind. I'll do it myself.

items.notes: Said calmly, mou ii desu politely turns down more food. As a question, mou ii? means 'ready?' or 'is that enough?'.

items.english: whatever; I don't care; it doesn't matter
items.use: Dismisses something as unimportant; to someone's face it can sound rude.

example.romaji: sonna koto, dou demo ii yo.
example.ja: そんなこと、どうでもいいよ。
example.english: I don't care about that.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna koto wa dou demo ii desu.
examplePolite.ja: そんなことはどうでもいいです。
examplePolite.english: That doesn't matter.

items.notes: Don't confuse with nan demo ii (anything is fine), the friendly way to say you have no preference.

items.use: Self-talk as you decide to let something go.

example.romaji: densha itchatta. maa ii ka, tsugi matou.
example.ja: 電車行っちゃった。まあいいか、次待とう。
example.english: Missed the train. Oh well, I'll wait for the next one.

items.english: so what?; is there a problem?
items.use: Cool, defensive comeback when someone points something out about you.

example.romaji: hitori de kita yo. sore ga nanika?
example.ja: 一人で来たよ。それが何か？
example.english: I came alone. So what?

examplePolite.romaji: hitori de kimashita kedo, sore ga nanika?
examplePolite.ja: 一人で来ましたけど、それが何か？
examplePolite.english: I came alone. Is there a problem?

items.notes: Sounds icy even in polite speech.

blocks.label: No no, come on
blocks.rationale: Deny or laugh off praise, ideas and claims.
blocks.interference: iya iya is modest; sore wa nai is a firm no.

items.english: no, no; not at all; oh, come on
items.use: Modest denial when you're praised or thanked; also brushes off a silly idea.

example.romaji: iya iya, sonna koto nai yo.
example.ja: いやいや、そんなことないよ。
example.english: No, no, not at all.

examplePolite.romaji: iya iya, sonna koto nai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: いやいや、そんなことないですよ。
examplePolite.english: Oh no, not at all.

items.notes: In polite talk, ie ie is a softer choice.

items.english: no way; that's not fair; that won't happen
items.use: Rejects an idea as impossible or unfair.

example.romaji: e, ashita made? sore wa nai yo.
example.ja: え、明日まで？それはないよ。
example.english: What, by tomorrow? No way.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita made desu ka? sore wa nai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 明日までですか？それはないですよ。
examplePolite.english: By tomorrow? That's not fair.

items.english: no way; not at all; nope
items.use: Laughs off a suggestion, like being asked if you're dating someone.

example.romaji: kanojo? nai nai, tada no tomodachi.
example.ja: 彼女？ないない、ただの友達。
example.english: Girlfriend? No way, she's just a friend.

examplePolite.romaji: nai nai, tada no tomodachi desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: ないない、ただの友達ですよ。
examplePolite.english: No, no, she's just a friend.

items.notes: Also said while searching: 'it's not here, not here'.

items.use: Playful disbelief when someone flatters you or brags.

example.romaji: mata mata, joudan bakkari.
example.ja: またまた、冗談ばっかり。
example.english: Oh, come on, always joking.

examplePolite.romaji: mata mata, joudan deshou?
examplePolite.ja: またまた、冗談でしょう？
examplePolite.english: Oh, come on, you're joking.

items.notes: Not 'again' here, though mata alone means again.

blocks.label: Shouts and exclamations
blocks.rationale: Recognize the quick outbursts of surprise, scolding and frustration.
blocks.interference: kora scolds; it isn't a general 'hey'.

items.use: Tell someone to stop, from playful teasing to real danger.

example.romaji: chotto, yamete yo! kusuguttai!
example.ja: ちょっと、やめてよ！くすぐったい！
example.english: Hey, stop it! That tickles!

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, sore, yamete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、それ、やめてください。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, please stop that.

items.notes: yamero is the harsh command form you'll hear in dramas; yamete is softer and used by anyone.

items.use: Surprise or delight at something you see, like a view, a gift or food arriving.

example.romaji: waa, kirei! mite, umi ga mieru yo.
example.ja: わあ、きれい！見て、海が見えるよ。
example.english: Wow, beautiful! Look, you can see the sea.

examplePolite.romaji: waa, kirei desu ne! umi ga miemasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: わあ、きれいですね！海が見えますよ。
examplePolite.english: Wow, how beautiful! You can see the sea.

items.notes: uwa! leans toward shock or disgust; waa is usually pleasant.

items.use: An adult catching a child or pet misbehaving; playful between friends.

example.romaji: kora! sonna tokoro ni nobotcha dame!
example.ja: こら！そんなところに登っちゃダメ！
example.english: Hey! You can't climb up there!

items.notes: Don't use it to call adults; ooi is the neutral calling 'hey'.

items.use: Muttered in frustration when something goes wrong; in slang it also intensifies, as in kuso muzui (damn hard).

example.romaji: kuso, mata maketa! mou ikkai!
example.ja: クソ、また負けた！もう一回！
example.english: Damn, lost again! One more time!

items.notes: Literally 'dung'. Good to recognize, risky to say: it sounds harsh, especially from a learner.

blocks.label: Giving your opinion
blocks.rationale: Ask what someone thinks, then agree or hedge.
blocks.interference: A drawn-out uun is 'hmm', but a quick dropping uun means no.

items.use: Ask someone's opinion; answer X to omou (I think X) or sou omou.

example.romaji: kono fuku, dou omou? chotto hade kana.
example.ja: この服、どう思う？ちょっと派手かな。
example.english: What do you think of this outfit? Too loud?

examplePolite.romaji: kono fuku, dou omoimasu ka? chotto hade deshou ka.
examplePolite.ja: この服、どう思いますか？ちょっと派手でしょうか。
examplePolite.english: What do you think of this outfit? Is it a bit loud?

items.notes: Use dou (how), not nani (what): nani o omou? sounds wrong.

items.use: Fills the pause while you think, or softens a no; a long, falling uun often means the answer is no.

example.romaji: uun, dou shiyou kana. mada kimete nai.
example.ja: うーん、どうしようかな。まだ決めてない。
example.english: Hmm, what should I do? I haven't decided yet.

examplePolite.romaji: uun, dou shimashou ka ne. mada kimete imasen.
examplePolite.ja: うーん、どうしましょうかね。まだ決めていません。
examplePolite.english: Hmm, what to do. I haven't decided yet.

items.notes: Said short with a drop (ううん, also uun), it means no; un alone is yeah.

items.use: Agree with an opinion; sou omowanai is 'I don't think so'.

example.romaji: un, watashi mo sou omou.
example.ja: うん、私もそう思う。
example.english: Yeah, I think so too.

examplePolite.romaji: hai, watashi mo sou omoimasu.
examplePolite.ja: はい、私もそう思います。
examplePolite.english: Yes, I think so too.

items.notes: Usually with mo: watashi mo sou omou, 'I think so too'.

items.english: well, who knows; come on, let's go
items.use: With a shrug it dodges a question you can't answer; said briskly it gets people moving.

example.romaji: saa, doko itta n darou. shiranai.
example.ja: さあ、どこ行ったんだろう。知らない。
example.english: Who knows where he went. No idea.

examplePolite.romaji: saa, chotto wakarimasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: さあ、ちょっとわかりませんね。
examplePolite.english: Hmm, I'm not really sure.

items.notes: A bare saa can sound dismissive; add chotto wakaranai to soften it.

items.english: hard to say; I can't really say
items.use: When you can't judge yet or won't commit; also for a feeling that's hard to put into words.

example.romaji: mada hajimatta bakari da kara, nantomo ienai na.
example.ja: まだ始まったばかりだから、なんとも言えないな。
example.english: It's only just started, so it's hard to say.

examplePolite.romaji: mada hajimatta bakari na node, nantomo iemasen.
examplePolite.ja: まだ始まったばかりなので、なんとも言えません。
examplePolite.english: It's only just started, so I can't really say.

items.notes: nantomo ienai aji, 'a taste you can't describe', is praise.

blocks.label: What do you mean
blocks.rationale: Ask for an explanation or what someone is getting at.
blocks.interference: nan no hanashi and nan no koto are near twins; dou iu koto asks for the reason.

items.english: what do you mean?; what's going on?
items.use: Ask someone to explain something confusing or surprising; said sharply, it demands an explanation.

example.romaji: e, chuushi? dou iu koto?
example.ja: え、中止？どういうこと？
example.english: Wait, cancelled? What do you mean?

examplePolite.romaji: e, chuushi desu ka? dou iu koto desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: え、中止ですか？どういうことですか？
examplePolite.english: Wait, it's cancelled? What do you mean?

items.notes: dou iu imi? asks only what a word or sentence means.

items.use: Ask when you've lost the thread, or play dumb about something you'd rather not discuss.

example.romaji: e, nan no hanashi? zenzen shiranai kedo.
example.ja: え、何の話？全然知らないけど。
example.english: Huh, what are you talking about? I've no idea.

examplePolite.romaji: e, nan no hanashi desu ka? zenzen shiranai n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: え、何の話ですか？全然知らないんですけど。
examplePolite.english: Huh, what are you talking about? I've no idea.

items.notes: Joining a group, ask nan no hanashi shiteru no? (what are you all talking about?).

items.english: what do you mean?; what are you talking about?
items.use: Asks what someone is referring to; often feigned innocence when accused of something.

example.romaji: nan no koto? watashi, nani mo shiranai yo.
example.ja: 何のこと？私、何も知らないよ。
example.english: What are you talking about? I don't know anything.

examplePolite.romaji: nan no koto desu ka? watashi wa nani mo shirimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 何のことですか？私は何も知りません。
examplePolite.english: What do you mean? I don't know anything.

items.notes: Close to nan no hanashi; nan no koto points at one thing someone mentioned.

items.english: what do you want?; what is it?
items.use: Asked when someone calls you or turns up; can sound curt depending on tone.

example.romaji: nanka you? ima chotto isogashii n da kedo.
example.ja: 何か用？今ちょっと忙しいんだけど。
example.english: What is it? I'm a bit busy right now.

examplePolite.romaji: nanika goyou desu ka? ima chotto isogashii n desu ga.
examplePolite.ja: 何かご用ですか？今ちょっと忙しいんですが。
examplePolite.english: Can I help you? I'm a bit busy right now.

items.notes: nanika you? is the same, a touch less blunt. Staff use the polite form to mean 'Can I help you?'.

blocks.label: Correcting a mix-up
blocks.rationale: Say 'no, that's not it' and push back on a plan.
blocks.interference: sou ja nakute corrects what was meant; sou wa ikanai refuses an easy way out.

items.english: no, I mean...; that's not what I meant
items.use: Correct a misunderstanding, then say what you actually meant.

example.romaji: sou ja nakute, ashita no hanashi da yo.
example.ja: そうじゃなくて、明日の話だよ。
example.english: No, I mean tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: sou ja nakute, ashita no hanashi desu.
examplePolite.ja: そうじゃなくて、明日の話です。
examplePolite.english: No, I'm talking about tomorrow.

items.notes: In formal talk: sou de wa nakute.

items.use: Quick correction, often with a hand wave, when someone guesses or does it wrong.

example.romaji: chigau chigau, sotchi ja nakute kotchi!
example.ja: 違う違う、そっちじゃなくてこっち！
example.english: No, no, not that one, this one!

items.notes: Politely, a single iie, chigaimasu. chigau also means 'different'.

items.english: it's not that simple; not so fast
items.use: Push back when someone suggests an easy way out or tries to get away with something.

example.romaji: yasumitai kedo, sou wa ikanai n da yo.
example.ja: 休みたいけど、そうはいかないんだよ。
example.english: I'd love a day off, but it's not that simple.

examplePolite.romaji: yasumitai n desu kedo, sou wa ikanai n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 休みたいんですけど、そうはいかないんですよ。
examplePolite.english: I'd love a day off, but it's not that simple.

items.notes: iku here means 'go smoothly', as in umaku ikanai (it isn't going well).

blocks.label: Getting attention
blocks.rationale: Get someone's attention before you speak, and respond when they show you something.
blocks.interference: ano alone is just 'um'; ooi calls to someone far away.

items.use: Soft opener before you tell someone something; common with kids and partners.

example.romaji: ano ne, kyou gakkou de omoshiroi koto atta no.
example.ja: あのね、今日学校で面白いことあったの。
example.english: You know what? Something funny happened at school today.

items.notes: ano alone is a hesitant 'um'; ano ne and ano sa announce you have something to say.

items.use: Casual opener before a question or news among friends; more direct than ano ne.

example.romaji: ano sa, ashita hima? eiga ikanai?
example.ja: あのさ、明日暇？映画行かない？
example.english: Hey, are you free tomorrow? Want to see a movie?

items.notes: With people you'd speak politely to, open with ano, sumimasen instead.

items.english: listen to this; hear me out
items.use: Grab a friend's attention before news or a rant; chotto kiite yo is more insistent.
items.politeJa: ちょっと聞いてください

example.romaji: chotto kiite! kinou sugoi koto ga atta no.
example.ja: ちょっと聞いて！昨日すごいことがあったの。
example.english: Listen to this! Something crazy happened yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto kiite kudasai. kinou sugoi koto ga atta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと聞いてください。昨日すごいことがあったんです。
examplePolite.english: Listen to this. Something amazing happened yesterday.

items.notes: kiku also means 'ask': chotto kiite ii? is 'can I ask you something?'

items.use: Call to someone far off or not paying attention; also 'anyone there?'

example.romaji: ooi, kotchi da yo! hayaku oide!
example.ja: おーい、こっちだよ！早くおいで！
example.english: Hey, over here! Come on!

items.notes: To get a stranger's attention, say sumimasen instead.

items.english: let's see; let me have a look
items.use: Said as you lean in to look at something someone wants to show you.

example.romaji: dore dore, chotto misete.
example.ja: どれどれ、ちょっと見せて。
example.english: Let's see, show me.

examplePolite.romaji: dore dore, chotto misete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: どれどれ、ちょっと見せてください。
examplePolite.english: Let's see, may I have a look?

items.notes: Sounds a little like a parent or teacher checking something.

blocks.label: Things you just learned
blocks.rationale: React to news, or to something you missed.
blocks.interference: shiranakatta is for facts; kizukanakatta is for things you failed to see.

items.english: I didn't know (that); I had no idea
items.use: React to news or a fact that surprises you, often after e, honto?

example.romaji: e, kekkon shita no? zenzen shiranakatta!
example.ja: え、結婚したの？全然知らなかった！
example.english: What, you got married? I had no idea!

examplePolite.romaji: e, kekkon sareta n desu ka? zenzen shirimasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: え、結婚されたんですか？全然知りませんでした。
examplePolite.english: Oh, you got married? I had no idea.

items.notes: shiranai (present) is 'I don't know'; use the past for news you've just heard.

items.english: oh, so that's it; now I get it
items.use: Said when something finally makes sense, often half to yourself.

example.romaji: aa, sou iu koto ka! yatto wakatta.
example.ja: ああ、そういうことか！やっと分かった。
example.english: Oh, so that's it! I finally get it.

examplePolite.romaji: aa, sou iu koto desu ne. yatto wakarimashita.
examplePolite.ja: ああ、そういうことですね。やっと分かりました。
examplePolite.english: Ah, so that's what it is. Now I understand.

items.notes: Close to naruhodo; the ka falls, so it isn't a question.

items.english: I didn't notice; I didn't realize
items.use: When you missed something right in front of you; also an apology for an oversight.

example.romaji: gomen, kiteta no? zenzen kizukanakatta.
example.ja: ごめん、来てたの？全然気づかなかった。
example.english: Sorry, you were here? I didn't notice at all.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, irasshatta n desu ka. zenzen kizukimasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、いらっしゃったんですか。全然気づきませんでした。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, you were here? I didn't notice at all.

items.notes: shiranakatta is for facts you didn't know; kizukanakatta is for things you failed to see.

blocks.label: Emergencies and getting help
blocks.rationale: Call for help or an ambulance, warn of an earthquake, and show where it hurts.
blocks.interference: tasukete is for danger; tetsudatte is help with a task.

items.use: Shout for help in danger; to a friend it can also be a jokey 'help me out'.

example.romaji: dareka tasukete! hito ga taoreta!
example.ja: 誰か助けて！人が倒れた！
example.english: Somebody help! Someone's collapsed!

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, tasukete kudasai! hito ga taoremashita!
examplePolite.ja: すみません、助けてください！人が倒れました！
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, please help! Someone's collapsed!

items.notes: For everyday help with a task, tetsudatte (give me a hand) is more natural.

items.use: Ask a bystander to call; the number in Japan is 119, which also reaches the fire service.
items.kana: きゅうきゅうしゃをよんで
items.politeJa: 救急車を呼んでください

example.romaji: hayaku kyuukyuusha o yonde! ishiki ga nai.
example.ja: 早く救急車を呼んで！意識がない。
example.english: Quick, call an ambulance! She's unconscious.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, kyuukyuusha o yonde kudasai!
examplePolite.ja: すみません、救急車を呼んでください！
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, please call an ambulance!

items.notes: Police is 110 (keisatsu); 119 is ambulance and fire.

items.use: Shouted when the shaking starts; announcements and teachers use jishin desu.

example.romaji: a, jishin da! hayaku tsukue no shita ni!
example.ja: あっ、地震だ！早く机の下に！
example.english: Whoa, earthquake! Quick, under the table!

examplePolite.romaji: jishin desu! tsukue no shita ni haitte kudasai!
examplePolite.ja: 地震です！机の下に入ってください！
examplePolite.english: Earthquake! Get under your desks!

items.notes: The early-warning alert on phones and TV says jishin desu, jishin desu.

items.use: Point and say it at a clinic or pharmacy; the doctor asks doko ga itai desu ka? (where does it hurt?).

example.romaji: kinou kara koko ga itai n da.
example.ja: 昨日からここが痛いんだ。
example.english: It's been hurting here since yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou kara koko ga itai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日からここが痛いんです。
examplePolite.english: It's been hurting here since yesterday.

items.notes: itai! alone is 'ouch!'; swap koko for a body part: atama ga itai (my head hurts).

blocks.label: Lost and getting around
blocks.rationale: Say you're lost and ask the way.
blocks.interference: None.

items.english: where am I?; where is this?
items.use: Muttered on waking up somewhere strange or getting lost; ask strangers with the polite form.

example.romaji: are, koko doko? machigaeta kamo.
example.ja: あれ、ここどこ？間違えたかも。
example.english: Huh, where am I? I might've gone the wrong way.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, koko wa doko desu ka? chizu de oshiete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、ここはどこですか？地図で教えてください。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, where is this? Could you show me on the map?

items.use: Tell a passer-by or a friend on the phone that you don't know where you are.

example.romaji: gomen, michi ni mayotta. chotto okureru.
example.ja: ごめん、道に迷った。ちょっと遅れる。
example.english: Sorry, I got lost. I'll be a bit late.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, michi ni mayotte shimatte, sukoshi okuremasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、道に迷ってしまって、少し遅れます。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I got lost, so I'll be a little late.

items.notes: mayou alone also means 'can't decide': dotchi ni suru ka mayotteru.

items.use: Ask a stranger or staff for directions after naming the place: X made dou ikeba ii desu ka?
items.ja: どう行けばいいですか
items.kana: どういけばいいですか

example.romaji: sumimasen, eki made dou ikeba ii desu ka?
example.ja: すみません、駅までどう行けばいいですか？
example.english: Excuse me, how do I get to the station?

items.notes: With friends: dou ikeba ii? Simpler still: eki wa doko desu ka? (where's the station?).

items.use: A common late-night problem: trains stop around midnight, leaving a taxi, a net cafe or a long walk.

example.romaji: yabai, shuuden nogashita. takushii shika nai.
example.ja: やばい、終電逃した。タクシーしかない。
example.english: Crap, I missed the last train. It's a taxi now.

examplePolite.romaji: shuuden o nogashita node, takushii de kaerimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 終電を逃したので、タクシーで帰ります。
examplePolite.english: I missed the last train, so I'll take a taxi home.

items.notes: shuuden is the last train; the first one of the day is shihatsu.

blocks.label: Broken or lost things
blocks.rationale: Report that something broke, won't work, or went missing.
blocks.interference: nakushita is lost for good; wasuremono shita is left somewhere.

items.use: Say a thing has broken or stopped working.

example.romaji: aa, sumaho kowareta. gamen ga tsukanai.
example.ja: ああ、スマホ壊れた。画面がつかない。
example.english: Ugh, my phone's broken. The screen won't turn on.

examplePolite.romaji: sumaho ga kowaremashita. gamen ga tsukimasen.
examplePolite.ja: スマホが壊れました。画面がつきません。
examplePolite.english: My phone broke. The screen won't turn on.

items.notes: kowasu is 'break (something)': kowashichatta, 'I broke it'.

items.english: it won't work; it won't move; it's stuck
items.use: For machines that won't run, doors or lids that won't budge, or a body part you can't move.

example.romaji: kono kopiiki, mata ugokanai yo.
example.ja: このコピー機、また動かないよ。
example.english: This copier's not working again.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, kono kopiiki ga ugokanai n desu ga.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、このコピー機が動かないんですが。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, this copier isn't working.

items.notes: For screens and lights that won't come on, use tsukanai.

items.english: I left something behind; I forgot something
items.use: When you realize you left something at home, on a train or in a shop.

example.romaji: a, wasuremono shita! chotto modoru ne.
example.ja: あ、忘れ物した！ちょっと戻るね。
example.english: Oh, I forgot something! I'll run back.

examplePolite.romaji: a, wasuremono o shimashita. chotto modorimasu.
examplePolite.ja: あ、忘れ物をしました。ちょっと戻ります。
examplePolite.english: Oh, I left something behind. I'll just go back.

items.notes: On trains you'll hear owasuremono in announcements reminding you not to leave things behind.
